digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-18
digests.theme: Today is a state-sensitive intervention logic versus platform hygiene day. The most relevant paper is Exploratory decoding of TMS-EEG: Predicting TEP response to intermittent and continuous theta burst stimulation, because it directly attacks one of the core bottlenecks in noninvasive neuromodulation: whether pre-stimulation brain state can forecast protocol-specific cortical response instead of treating variability as noise. The strongest adjacent computational paper is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder, which is not an intervention study but does try to connect altered state transitions to an explicit control-energy framing. The most practically useful methods paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation, because sham quality and coupling reproducibility are still underappreciated failure points in human ultrasound work. The clinically interesting but still caution-heavy paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation connectivity related to apathy outcomes in Parkinson's disease.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Exploratory decoding of TMS-EEG: Predicting TEP response to intermittent and continuous theta burst stimulation. In a randomized single-blind crossover study of 15 healthy men, the authors ask whether resting-state EEG features before stimulation can predict changes in six TMS-evoked-potential components after intermittent or continuous theta-burst stimulation over left primary motor cortex. Lasso and CatBoost both beat a random-guessing baseline, with protocol- and component-specific differences in which model worked best. This is still small and exploratory, but it is the right kind of question, because it treats stimulation response as state-dependent and partially decodable rather than intrinsically capricious.

The second paper is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Using co-activation-pattern analysis plus network control theory in 198 OCD patients and 109 controls, the authors report more occupancy of ventral-attention and somatomotor states with default-mode suppression, less persistence of a frontoparietal-dominant state, and altered transition energetics across those states. The useful part is not the psychiatry branding. It is the attempt to tie rapid state switching to an explicit energetic-control framing and then test virtual perturbations that partially normalize the abnormal dynamics.

The third paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation. The paper focuses on coupling hardware rather than physiology, but that is exactly why it matters. The authors build matched gel-plastic verum and sham couplers and show that one configuration stays acoustically transparent while an air-gap sham strongly attenuates transmitted energy without obvious tactile or visual differences. Human ultrasound neuromodulation still has too much sloppiness around blinding and coupling, so a paper that hardens that layer is more useful than another vague efficacy teaser.

The fourth paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation connectivity related to apathy outcomes in Parkinson's disease. In 53 Parkinson's patients with bilateral STN DBS, the authors use normative structural-connectivity modeling to link worsening apathy to asymmetric pathways involving right dentatorubrothalamic and supplementary-motor trajectories and left anteromedial-STN connections to anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal regions. The holdout correlation is stronger than many connectomic side-effect papers manage, but the sample is still modest, the model is normative rather than patient-specific, and the result should guide caution and hypothesis-building more than programming dogma.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are the ones that make neuromodulation less hand-wavy. The TMS-EEG study says baseline physiology may contain protocol-specific predictive signal. The OCD network-control study says psychiatric state dynamics can be framed as transitions with differing energetic costs rather than just altered static connectivity. The LIFU coupling paper says human ultrasound needs better sham and coupling discipline if it wants trustworthy causal claims. The Parkinson apathy paper says side effects may be connectomically structured, but still needs more patient-specific and prospective validation before it becomes programming doctrine.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-17
digests.theme: Today is a parameter-specific circuit modulation versus decorative network language day. The most relevant paper is Frequency-dependent modulation of human reward circuitry: A comparative study of theta, gamma, and high-frequency temporal interference, because it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to test whether noninvasive deep-target stimulation actually behaves differently when you change the control frequency instead of just changing the branding. The strongest network-development paper is Mapping the spatiotemporal continuum of structural connectivity development across the human connectome in youth, which gives a useful developmental scaffold for thinking about adolescent intervention timing and heterogeneity. The best cautionary neuromodulation paper is Sensory Function Improves With Subthalamic Nucleus Stimulation in Parkinson's: A Network Analysis, because it is clinically interesting and connectomically framed, but still exploratory enough that it should shape hypotheses more than programming doctrine.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Frequency-dependent modulation of human reward circuitry: A comparative study of theta, gamma, and high-frequency temporal interference. In 24 healthy adults, the authors applied individualized nucleus-accumbens-targeted temporal interference stimulation at 5, 40, or 130 hertz and acquired resting-state functional MRI before and after stimulation. The main result is a frequency-specific dissociation: there was no convincing local spontaneous-activity shift in nucleus accumbens across conditions, but 130 hertz selectively reduced nucleus-accumbens to medial-prefrontal connectivity, with individual local activity reduction tracking the degree of circuit decoupling. That is not yet a therapeutic result, but it is a much more concrete control-parameter paper than the usual vague deep-target neuromodulation claim.

The second paper is Mapping the spatiotemporal continuum of structural connectivity development across the human connectome in youth. Using diffusion MRI across three developmental cohorts, the authors argue that structural connectivity maturation follows a sensorimotor-to-association continuum, with earlier strengthening of sensorimotor-to-sensorimotor links and later strengthening of association-to-association links, crossing around age fifteen. The useful part is not just another developmental atlas. It is the claim that cognition and psychopathology map differently onto this maturation axis, especially in association cortex, which matters for developmental targeting logic and for not treating adolescence as one undifferentiated phase.

The third paper is Sensory Function Improves With Subthalamic Nucleus Stimulation in Parkinson's: A Network Analysis. In 21 Parkinson's patients with subthalamic deep brain stimulation, the authors relate stimulation locations and normative structural connectivity to changes in rubber-hand-illusion measures of sensory decision making. The provocative claim is that improvement tracks the associative-limbic subthalamic nucleus and bilateral prefrontal connectivity rather than purely motor circuitry. That is interesting because it pushes deep brain stimulation effects beyond motor-output framing, but the endpoint is unusual, the analysis is retrospective, and the network claims remain exploratory.

The fourth paper is Oscillatory network efficiency predicts mood and fatigue during sleep deprivation. This is adjacent rather than intervention-facing, but still worth preserving because it tries to model circadian and infradian fluctuations in network topology rather than treating sleep loss as a single static perturbation. The mechanism is still correlational, yet the paper is useful for state-dependent intervention logic because it frames vulnerability as time-varying and region-specific rather than globally homogeneous.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are the ones that make intervention logic more explicit. The temporal-interference study says parameter choice can matter at the circuit level even when local target readouts stay messy. The youth-connectome paper says developmental structural maturation is not uniform and that psychopathology-relevant variation concentrates in later-maturing association connections. The Parkinson network-analysis paper hints that subthalamic stimulation can shape sensory decision processes through associative-limbic and prefrontal circuitry, but the evidence is still exploratory. The sleep-deprivation paper adds a broader state-space reminder: if network efficiency itself oscillates with internal timing, then state-contingent neuromodulation should expect rhythmic moving targets rather than static baselines.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-16
digests.theme: Today is a generalizable decoding versus flimsy biomarker day. The most relevant paper is Multitarget brain implants enable generalized decoding of Parkinson’s disease symptoms from chronic home recordings, because it pushes adaptive deep brain stimulation away from single-band beta loyalty and toward symptom-specific decoding that actually generalizes across patients. The strongest biomarker-methods paper is Distinct Predictive and Recovery EEG Biomarkers of Motor Function after Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Subacute Stroke Patients, which makes the useful distinction between a feature that predicts who responds and a feature that tracks recovery once treatment is underway. The most important clinical caution paper is Safety and feasibility of combined anterior limb of the internal capsule–nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation in carefully selected children and adolescents with severe, treatment-refractory autism spectrum disorder: a single-arm pilot study, because it is ethically and clinically provocative but still far too uncontrolled to treat as efficacy evidence.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Multitarget brain implants enable generalized decoding of Parkinson’s disease symptoms from chronic home recordings. Across 16 Parkinson’s participants and more than 581 hours of home recordings from cortical and deep-brain implants, the authors train cross-patient machine-learning decoders for bradykinesia, tremor, and dyskinesia. The real advance is not just higher accuracy than beta power. It is that the models decode multiple symptoms, work without patient-specific retraining, and are framed as a bridge between adaptive DBS timing and connectomic steering.

The second paper is Distinct Predictive and Recovery EEG Biomarkers of Motor Function after Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Subacute Stroke Patients. Twelve subacute stroke patients received dual-mode noninvasive brain stimulation, and baseline EEG features were used to predict responder status while longitudinal EEG changes were tested against motor improvement. The useful result is conceptual: the feature that best predicts response at baseline, ipsilesional temporal beta power, is not the same feature that tracks recovery over time, which was relative delta power change at ipsilesional occipital cortex. That is a cleaner intervention-logic claim than the usual biomarker pileup.

The third paper is Safety and feasibility of combined anterior limb of the internal capsule–nucleus accumbens deep brain stimulation in carefully selected children and adolescents with severe, treatment-refractory autism spectrum disorder: a single-arm pilot study. Twelve pediatric autism patients underwent bilateral ALIC-NAc DBS, 11 completed six months, and exploratory symptom scores improved without serious intervention-related adverse events. This is worth attention because pediatric circuit intervention in severe autism is a real boundary case for neuromodulation, and the paper at least reports tolerability and exploratory local field potential changes. But the design is open-label, single-arm, and small enough that efficacy inference is still fragile.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today reject the lazy idea that one biomarker, one target, or one average score is enough. The Parkinson preprint says adaptive control should decode symptom-specific states from richer multisite signals. The stroke paper says prediction features and recovery-tracking features can be different objects and should be treated that way. The autism pilot says that once neuromodulation enters severe developmental psychiatry, feasibility and safety reporting matter, but uncontrolled symptom improvements still do not earn mechanistic confidence. Different modalities, same lesson: intervention logic gets stronger when state estimation, control target, and evidentiary standard are kept separate.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-15
digests.theme: Today is a network-targeting-and-controller-design day. The most relevant paper is Combinatorial effects of multi-site stimulation on depression-related brain regions: clinical data analysis and predictive modeling, because it directly tests how bilateral and multi-target deep brain stimulation combine inside depression-relevant networks instead of pretending multiple contacts simply add. The strongest network-guided noninvasive paper is A meta-analysis suggests that TMS targeting the hippocampal network selectively improves episodic memory, which is useful less as therapy hype and more as evidence that a connectivity-defined target class can produce domain-selective effects when the task logic is right. The most useful computational neuroengineering paper is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation, because it treats adaptive stimulation as a patient-specific control problem rather than a one-biomarker religion.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Combinatorial effects of multi-site stimulation on depression-related brain regions: clinical data analysis and predictive modeling. Three treatment-resistant depression participants received bilateral subcallosal cingulate and ventral capsule or ventral striatum stimulation while stereo-EEG sampled prefrontal depression networks. The important result is not clinical efficacy. It is that bilateral and cross-target combinations were usually additive or sub-additive, with region of interest contributing more to the interaction class than target name alone. That matters because multi-target depression DBS is often discussed as if more stimulation automatically means more network leverage, and this paper says the interaction structure is more constrained than that.

The second paper is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation. Across 19 Parkinson's patients and 35 sessions, the authors used patient-specific EEG or epidural ECoG features to decode drawing-task motor performance under DBS on and off conditions. The headline is not just that decoding works in many sessions. It is that the paper separates informative biomarkers from controllable ones and shows that some decodable signals would still be bad adaptive-DBS control variables. That is a healthier framing than the usual biomarker hunting.

The third paper is A meta-analysis suggests that TMS targeting the hippocampal network selectively improves episodic memory. Across 38 studies and 1,009 participants, hippocampal indirectly targeted stimulation produced a moderate positive effect on episodic memory, near-zero effects on non-memory cognition, stronger effects for recollection-heavy tasks, and stronger effects when stimulation came before the task instead of between encoding and retrieval. This does not magically validate every hippocampal-network TMS protocol, but it is one of the cleaner signs that network-guided targeting can produce functionally selective effects when the behavioral assay actually matches the circuit claim.
digests.takeaway: The strongest pattern today is that useful neuromodulation papers are getting better when they stop treating targets, biomarkers, and stimulation combinations as self-justifying objects. The depression DBS paper asks how effects compose across a network. The Parkinson paper asks whether a decoded feature is actually suitable for control. The hippocampal-network TMS meta-analysis asks whether a connectivity-guided intervention produces selective behavioral effects instead of generic uplift. Different modalities, same demand: intervention logic has to match network structure, state measurement, and task design.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-14
digests.theme: Today is a closed-loop-and-circuit-control day. The most relevant paper is Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children, because it combines pediatric intracranial recordings, online prediction of impending attentional lapses, rescue stimulation, and a scalp-signature bridge toward noninvasive translation. The strongest mechanistic network paper is Beyond seizure control: Identifying deficits in cognitive networks in absence epilepsy, which links cognitive inflexibility and seizure burden to the same thalamic-prefrontal circuit and then perturbs that circuit directly. The most useful computational framing paper is Fundamental questions on closed-loop neuromodulation: a control theory perspective, which is not an empirical breakthrough but does a good job naming the design constraints most closed-loop neuromod papers prefer to blur.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children. At the level accessible here, the core result is that intracranial recordings during an attentional set-shifting task were used to train classifiers that predicted impending delays in attention shifting, and stimulation delivered in response to those predicted lapses improved eye-tracking, reaction-time, and accuracy readouts. The translational hook is that simultaneous electroencephalography reportedly exposed corresponding scalp signatures that then supported noninvasive modulation in healthy participants. If the full methods hold up, this is a serious example of task-linked closed-loop intervention rather than generic stimulation branding.

The second paper is Beyond seizure control: Identifying deficits in cognitive networks in absence epilepsy. This is preclinical, but it is exactly the right kind of preclinical paper: not just another seizure-suppression story, but a circuit account tying absence seizures, cognitive flexibility deficits, altered cortical inhibition, and thalamic reuniens to medial prefrontal pathway dysfunction into one mechanistic package. The strongest detail accessible here is that targeted stimulation of the thalamic-prefrontal pathway reportedly reduced seizure incidence and improved reversal-learning behavior. That makes it useful both as epilepsy mechanism work and as a model for intervention logic that tries to fix a shared circuit cause instead of separately treating symptoms.

The third paper is Fundamental questions on closed-loop neuromodulation: a control theory perspective. This is a perspective and synthesis piece, not a data paper, so it should not be oversold. Still, it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to say out loud what is wrong with most closed-loop neuromodulation claims: the plant is partially observed and under-actuated, nonstationarity is normal, stimulation confounds measurement, and hard safety constraints need to be architected in rather than stapled on later. The useful shift is from naive set-point control rhetoric toward therapeutic-window regulation under uncertainty.
digests.takeaway: The strongest scouting pattern today is that useful neuromodulation work is converging on the same demand from different directions: stop treating stimulation as a generic dose and start treating it as a state-dependent intervention on a circuit with measurable constraints. The pediatric attention paper is the most exciting translationally because it pairs online prediction with rescue stimulation. The absence-epilepsy paper is the mechanistic anchor because it names a shared circuit cause and perturbs it. The control-theory perspective is the cleanup crew because it says, correctly, that none of this becomes trustworthy unless nonstationarity, partial observability, and safety architecture are treated as central rather than optional.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-13
digests.theme: Today is a pathways-state-and-sensing day. The most relevant paper is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression, because it tries to replace coarse targeting folklore with an explicit structural route account for how dorsolateral prefrontal stimulation may reach subgenual depression circuitry. The strongest adjacent mechanistic paper is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity, which argues that local phase is not enough and that transient network state materially changes stimulation effects. The most useful methods paper is Reliability and signal comparison of OPM-MEG, fMRI & iEEG in a repeated movie viewing paradigm, which matters because better noninvasive state measurement is part of whether future adaptive neuromodulation claims deserve belief.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression. The paper argues that effective depression TMS sites are not just those with the right resting correlation to subgenual cingulate, but those with shorter and more plausible polysynaptic white-matter communication routes into that deeper circuit. According to the accessible abstract, modeled route length explained treatment response in two independent cohorts and also tracked the efficacy of functional-MRI-guided targeting. That is still a proxy story rather than direct propagation measurement, but it is a more serious mechanistic framing than anti-subgenual sloganism.

The second paper is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity. This is a whole-brain modeling paper, not a clinical trial, but it is exactly the kind of computational-control work that helps intervention logic. The authors argue that the same pulse can have different effects not only because of local oscillatory phase but also because the brain is occupying different transient functional-connectivity states. Their machine-learning comparison suggests that network-aware state descriptors improve prediction of stimulation effects by up to about forty percent and that perturbations can trigger global state switching rather than merely local response changes.

The third paper is Reliability and signal comparison of OPM-MEG, fMRI & iEEG in a repeated movie viewing paradigm. This is a measurement paper, but a useful one. It asks whether optically pumped magnetometer MEG gives reproducible stimulus-driven signals and whether those signals line up with both functional MRI and intracranial EEG. The answer appears to be yes, especially in lower frequency bands and especially in visual and auditory regions. That does not prove OPM-MEG is ready to run psychiatric closed loops, but it does make it a more credible future state-estimation tool than a sensor stack that only agrees with itself.
digests.takeaway: The strongest papers today all attack a different weak point in neuromodulation logic. One improves the propagation story, one improves the state story, and one improves the sensing story. The white-matter paper is the most directly useful because it gives depression TMS a more explicit circuit-communication frame. The dynamic-functional-connectivity paper is the most conceptually important for closed-loop control because it treats network state as part of the controller state. And the OPM paper matters because without trustworthy noninvasive measurement, a lot of adaptive-stimulation rhetoric stays decorative.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-12
digests.theme: Today is a causal-targeting and measurement-rigor day. The most relevant paper is A visual cortex origin of trauma memory intrusions: integrated evidence from TMS and fMRI, because it does more than wave at PTSD circuitry. It tests a concrete causal target and claims that low-frequency visual-cortex stimulation can reduce intrusion frequency, vividness, and emotional intensity while sparing gist memory. The strongest adjacent network paper is Altered flow of information in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, which is not an intervention paper but does provide a directed-information framing that could matter for developmental targeting logic. The strongest methods paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation, which matters because human ultrasound neuromodulation still needs better sham discipline more than it needs more soft positive stories.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is A visual cortex origin of trauma memory intrusions: integrated evidence from TMS and fMRI. Using a trauma-film paradigm in healthy participants, the authors combined functional MRI with one-hertz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to early visual cortex versus vertex control. They report reduced intrusion frequency, vividness, and emotional intensity over the next seven days after visual-cortex stimulation, while recognition of episodic gist was preserved. The mechanistic claim is that intrusive episodes are tracked more tightly by middle-frontal-gyrus to occipital-visual-cortex interactions than by the usual limbic-prefrontal story. If that result is solid, it is a more intervention-usable framing of intrusive memory than generic PTSD network rhetoric.

The second paper is Altered flow of information in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. In a reasonably sized developmental sample of 355 children, the authors estimate directed information flow using transfer entropy and report two opposing ADHD-related patterns: decreased flow converging on right visual cortex and right ventral anterior thalamus, and increased flow converging on right frontal operculum. The paper is useful mainly as a network-directionality paper, not as a biomarker solution. It sharpens the question of where information-routing bottlenecks may sit in ADHD, but it does not yet show that these measures are stable enough or intervention-linked enough to guide treatment.

The third paper is Acoustic Coupling for Double-Blind Human Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation. This is not glamorous, but it is worth preserving because the field badly needs credible sham infrastructure. The authors build gel-plastic coupling devices that are visually and tactually matched while either transmitting ultrasound efficiently or blocking it strongly through an internal air gap. At 0.50 megahertz, their preferred verum configuration shows low insertion loss and minimal beam distortion, while the sham shows roughly 31 decibels of insertion loss. That is exactly the kind of unsexy methods paper that makes future causal claims less embarrassing.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today either sharpen causal target logic or improve the credibility of future claims. The trauma-memory paper is the standout because it ties symptom change to a concrete perturbation target and a specific frontal-visual interaction story. The ADHD paper is useful because it treats directionality, not just connectivity strength, as the object of explanation. And the ultrasound paper matters because rigorous sham design is still one of the field's bottlenecks. Better control conditions are not decorative methods. They are part of whether the rest of the literature deserves belief.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-11
digests.theme: Today is a state-signals and targeting-discipline day. The most relevant paper is Subthalamic Signatures of Freezing while Turning in Parkinson’s Disease, because it moves one step closer to an actually usable adaptive-DBS logic by combining subthalamic beta-burst structure with turning kinematics instead of just narrating freezing after the fact. The strongest translational negative paper is Neurofunctional mechanisms of action of trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS) in children and adolescents with Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), because it does the useful thing and shows both neural and clinical non-effect under a better sham. The strongest clinical targeting paper in the mix remains Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Meige syndrome: mapping the optimal stimulation sites and network targets, which is not new to the repo but still matters because it combines local and network mapping with external validation.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Subthalamic Signatures of Freezing while Turning in Parkinson’s Disease. In thirteen Parkinson's disease patients with freezing of gait, the authors recorded subthalamic local field potentials synchronized with gait kinematics while patients were off medication and off stimulation. They compare regular turning, freezing while turning, unimpaired walking, and the transition period before turns. The useful result is that low-beta abnormalities appear both before and during freezing while turning, prolonged bursts mark the freezing state, and a simple mixed-effects logistic model using burst duration plus kinematic features reaches leave-one-subject-out AUROC around 0.84. That is not deployment-ready, but it is closer to a plausible control feature set than generic freezing biomarkers.

The second paper is Neurofunctional mechanisms of action of trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS) in children and adolescents with Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). This is a secondary mechanistic analysis from a larger multicenter United Kingdom randomized controlled trial that had already failed clinically. Across sixty-two children and adolescents with ADHD, real versus rigorous sham TNS showed no significant effects on fMRI activation during response inhibition, working memory, or sustained-attention tasks, and no task-performance benefit either. The value here is mostly negative and clarifying. Earlier pilot EEG optimism did not survive a larger sham-controlled fMRI test.

The third paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Meige syndrome: mapping the optimal stimulation sites and network targets. In sixty-five patients across two centers, the authors relate modeled stimulation geometry and network connectivity to long-term motor improvement, then validate the resulting maps in an independent cohort. The useful part is not that they found a sweet spot. Everyone finds a sweet spot. The useful part is that the local dorsolateral subthalamic target and the cerebellar and somatosensory network pattern both survive external validation reasonably well.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better neuromodulation papers either expose state structure or kill weak stories. The Parkinson's preprint is worth attention because it operationalizes a transition state with concrete LFP and kinematic features that could matter for adaptive control. The ADHD TNS paper is worth preserving because it says, pretty clearly, that a more rigorous trial found neither the expected brain effect nor clinical benefit. And the Meige DBS paper remains a reminder that targeting claims become much more interesting once they survive some version of external validation.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-10
digests.theme: Today is a network-physiology and stimulation-combination day. The most relevant paper is Brain-heart interactions in late-onset major depressive disorder revealed by multimodal HRV-driven fMRI, because it gives depression heterogeneity a more intervention-usable physiology frame than another generic resting-state case-control map. The strongest stimulation-methods paper is Trough-phase coupling of 40 Hz oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation with iTBS enhances corticospinal excitability and brain connectivity in healthy individuals, because it tests a concrete timing hypothesis instead of just piling one modality on top of another. The clinical translational paper that survived today is rTMS Modulates Static and Dynamic Brain Functional Networks in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: An EEG Microstate Study, which is interesting mainly as a network-readout paper, not because the clinical claim is already solid.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Brain-heart interactions in late-onset major depressive disorder revealed by multimodal HRV-driven fMRI. In twenty patients with late-onset major depressive disorder and twenty matched controls, the authors estimate time-varying autonomic regressors from simultaneous ECG and resting-state fMRI, then ask which brain regions track those autonomic fluctuations. The useful result is not just that depression touches the insula again. It is that right-insula, cingulate, and hippocampal coupling to autonomic dynamics appears altered, and right-insula response scales with symptom severity. That makes the paper more useful for interoceptive-state tracking and multimodal biomarker design than a standard resting-state paper.

The second paper is Trough-phase coupling of 40 Hz oscillatory transcranial direct current stimulation with iTBS enhances corticospinal excitability and brain connectivity in healthy individuals. In a randomized crossover study of eighteen healthy adults, the authors compare peak-phase and trough-phase coupling of oscillatory tDCS with intermittent theta burst stimulation, plus single-modality and sham controls. The main finding is that trough-phase coupling produces more sustained corticospinal facilitation and stronger late directed information flow in TMS-EEG than the alternatives. This is still a healthy-subject motor-cortex methods paper, but at least it tests a real phase-alignment hypothesis.

The third paper is rTMS Modulates Static and Dynamic Brain Functional Networks in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: An EEG Microstate Study. Thirty-two children with autism spectrum disorder were randomized to active or sham one-hertz dorsolateral prefrontal rTMS for nine weeks, with resting EEG and behavioral assessment before and after treatment. The paper did not show clear interaction effects in standard microstate timing parameters, but it did report stronger static connectivity and higher dynamic complexity across microstates after active stimulation. The mechanistic claim is modest, but the paper is still worth preserving because it treats network flexibility as a stimulation readout rather than just reporting symptom change.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better papers expose timing or physiology instead of hiding inside broad symptom labels. The strongest paper treats autonomic fluctuations as part of the depressive state representation and finds altered insula-centered coupling. The stimulation-methods paper shows that combined stimulation only becomes interesting when timing is part of the hypothesis. And the pediatric rTMS paper is mainly valuable as a reminder that network flexibility may be a better readout than whichever state-duration metric happens to be fashionable.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-09
digests.theme: Today is a mechanism-and-stratification day. The most relevant paper is Fronto-insular circuit mechanisms of accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation, because it does more than wave at connectivity. It builds a causal story for rapid antidepressant theta-burst effects across cell type, projection logic, mesoscale circuit engagement, and a limited human validation layer. The strongest network-stratification paper is Stable depression subtypes identified using functional connectome normative deviation models and their response to rTMS, because it takes heterogeneity seriously enough to ask whether a connectome-defined subtype actually changes treatment response. The main clinical benchmark resurfaced as Postapproval Study for Brain-Responsive Neurostimulation for Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy: Three-Year Efficacy and Interim Safety Results, which remains important as a seriousness check even though it is already in the repo. A second Cell paper, A cell type-specific mechanism driving the rapid antidepressant effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation, looked strong but overlapped heavily with the fronto-insular paper; I am logging it as citation material rather than preserving a full new note today.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Fronto-insular circuit mechanisms of accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation. In a mouse optogenetic model of prelimbic accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation, the authors report synapse-related transcriptional changes, more dendritic spines, stronger excitatory currents in prefrontal intratelencephalic neurons, and a fronto-insular circuit that appears necessary and sufficient for antidepressant-like effects. They then add a human bridge using stereo-EEG and resting-state fMRI to argue that insula engagement is not just a rodent curiosity. The useful read is not that one circuit has been solved. It is that aiTBS mechanism can be framed as target-site plasticity plus downstream fronto-insular recruitment rather than as generic prefrontal stimulation magic.

The second paper is Stable depression subtypes identified using functional connectome normative deviation models and their response to rTMS. Using over twelve hundred patients with depression and more than sixteen hundred healthy controls, the authors build individual connectome-deviation maps relative to a normative model and cluster them into two reproducible subtypes. Only one subtype showed significant anhedonia improvement after dorsolateral prefrontal rTMS. This is still preliminary and not yet the kind of stratification result that should drive clinical deployment, but it is more useful than decorative subtype talk because the subtype definition is tied to individual deviation structure and then tested against treatment response.

The third paper is Postapproval Study for Brain-Responsive Neurostimulation for Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy: Three-Year Efficacy and Interim Safety Results. This is not the most novel item today, and it already has a repo note, but it remains worth keeping in circulation. Across three years, real-world responsive neurostimulation outcomes were strong and broadly consistent across major onset-group splits. The paper does not solve detection-policy design or adaptive-control theory, but it is the sort of durable benchmark new closed-loop claims should have to face.
digests.takeaway: The common thread today is that good neuromodulation papers stop hiding behind averages and slogans. The strongest mechanistic paper traced accelerated theta-burst effects from prefrontal plasticity into a fronto-insular circuit that appears behaviorally necessary. The strongest stratification paper asked whether individual connectome-deviation structure actually changes response to rTMS and found an early but nontrivial signal. And the clinical benchmark paper reminded us that real-world durable performance, not just mechanism theater, is the standard adaptive systems eventually have to meet.

digests.theme: Today is a spatial biomarker, individualized targeting, geometry-hygiene, and direct-measurement day. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Spatial propagation of movement-related basal ganglia activity predicts parkinsonian motor state. Using multi-contact subthalamic recordings from sixty-three hemispheres during movement, the authors argue that movement-related high-frequency activity is not just stronger or weaker across patients. It also propagates through subthalamic space in band-specific ways, mainly along the inferior-superior axis, and the amount of propagation above one hundred and ten hertz inversely tracks dopaminergic motor improvement. The useful read is that future adaptive DBS may need spatially resolved state markers, not just one beta threshold from one contact pair.

The second paper is fNIRS-Guided neuronavigated rTMS augments naming recovery in subacute post-stroke aphasia: a double-blind randomized controlled trial. This is a small but real sham-controlled study in which the stimulation target was individualized from each patient's picture-naming activation map rather than chosen by template. Active stimulation improved naming more than sham and was associated with increased left dorsolateral prefrontal and Broca-area activation plus stronger connectivity between them. The sample is still small, and the target logic is task-activation-based rather than mechanistically deep, but this is more respectable than vague personalization rhetoric.

The third paper is Robustness of lead reconstruction for deep brain stimulation modelling and probabilistic mapping. This is not new to the repo, but it stayed worth preserving after today's scan because it hits the same pressure point from the methods side. Repeated postoperative CT scans in the same patients produced fairly robust group-level maps but much less stable individual volumes of tissue activation. That means the field is still too comfortable turning slightly shaky image registration into precise individualized programming stories.

The fourth paper is Direct mapping of neural activity via glutamate-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. This is not yet intervention evidence, but it is a provocative measurement paper. The authors combine chemical exchange saturation transfer with a dynamic model that explicitly accounts for BOLD contamination, then claim more spatially precise visual-cortex activation maps that are only explained when glutamate concentration changes are included. The right read is not that glutamate MRI has arrived as a ready biomarker. The right read is that more chemically specific state readouts may eventually improve how stimulation and network models are grounded.
digests.takeaway: The common thread today is that neuromodulation gets more serious when state and target are represented with more structure. In the subthalamic nucleus, movement-related activity may need to be treated as a spatially propagating process rather than a scalar oscillation. In noninvasive stimulation, individualized functional maps can help, but only when tested in a design strong enough to matter. In DBS modeling, geometric preprocessing still limits how precise individual claims should be. And in measurement, moving closer to neurotransmitter-linked signals may eventually make both targeting and control less hemodynamically hand-wavy.

digests.theme: Today is a target-legibility, neurochemical grounding, mapping-hygiene, and cautious adolescent-clinical-signal day. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Multimodal network localization of brain abnormalities and neuromodulation target identification in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The authors use coordinate-based network mapping to integrate structural abnormalities, executive-function findings, and emotion-processing findings in OCD, then compare those convergent maps against candidate neuromodulation targets. The useful part is that they do not pretend OCD is one monolithic abnormality blob. They recover partially dissociable networks that still converge on basal-ganglia circuitry, and they show that dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and supplementary motor area targets line up better with executive-network abnormalities than orbitofrontal cortex does. That is still a normative mapping exercise, not proof that these are the right intervention targets in any given patient.

The second paper is Linking human brain functional connectivity to underlying neurotransmission. Across six healthy cohorts using resting-state functional MRI and magnetoencephalography, the authors report that regional functional-connectivity variation aligns reproducibly with neurotransmitter receptor and transporter distributions, with a particularly prominent noradrenergic signature in a sensorimotor and posterior-insular network linked to autonomic arousal. This is not a stimulation paper, but it is intervention-relevant because it offers a cleaner biological bridge between systems-level connectivity claims and putative chemical levers.

The third paper is How Statistical Methods, Hemispheric Data and Masking Approaches Shape Probabilistic Sweet Spots in Deep Brain Stimulation. This is a useful anti-folklore paper. Using intraoperative stimulation-test data in Parkinson disease, the authors show that the shape and stability of probabilistic sweet spots depend heavily on the statistical test, cohort size, and whether hemispheres are merged. The main practical claim is that Bayesian t-tests stabilize sooner than the common Wilcoxon-based approaches, and that combining hemispheres can hide clinically relevant asymmetries rather than improve robustness.

The fourth paper is Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation (iTBS) Modulates Abnormal Brain Activity During Emotional Arousal in Adolescent Depression: A Pilot Study. This is the weakest note today, but still worth preserving. In adolescents with depression, the paper reports reduced superior and middle frontal responses during emotionally arousing video viewing, some symptom improvement after accelerated iTBS, and an exploratory association between target proximity to superior frontal abnormality and anxiety-score reduction. The right read is not precision-biomarker triumph. The right read is that adolescent TMS targeting remains suggestive and preliminary.
digests.takeaway: The common thread today is that target claims need better grounding at three levels. First, psychiatric abnormalities should be localized as networks with partially distinct functional roles, not as one big disease blob. Second, systems-level connectivity claims become more interesting when they can be related to underlying neurotransmitter architecture. Third, any map of “optimal stimulation sites” is only as trustworthy as the statistics and symmetry assumptions used to build it. The clinical pilot in adolescent depression is a decent reminder of what happens when those layers are still weak: you get a plausible target story with only modest evidence underneath it.

digests.theme: Today is a state-transition control, inverse-problem infrastructure, and stimulation-mechanism realism day. The most relevant paper is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder, because it does not just say OCD has altered dynamics. It tries to specify which state transitions become pathologically cheap, which become pathologically inefficient, and which neurotransmitter systems might shape that energy landscape. The strongest methods paper is A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics, because better source reconstruction is upstream of a lot of grand claims about network state, controllability, and stimulation targeting. The strongest direct stimulation-mechanism paper is Bifurcation of neural firing patterns driven by potassium dynamics and neuron-electrode geometry during high-frequency stimulation, because it explains abrupt firing-regime changes during high-frequency stimulation as a coupled geometry-plus-extracellular-ion problem rather than a one-line conduction-block slogan. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Neurochemically informed network control theory reveals energetic dysregulation of altered brain state dynamics in obsessive-compulsive disorder. In a fairly large resting-state fMRI cohort, the authors combine co-activation-pattern state analysis with network control theory and then map transition energetics onto neurotransmitter-related gradients. Their headline claim is that OCD is not just noisier or more variable. It is organized around a maladaptive cycle in which some default-mode to ventral-attention or somatomotor shifts become pathologically cheap, while another repetitive transition pattern remains inefficient in a way that still tracks symptoms. The attractive part is the intervention framing. The risky part is that the neurochemical layer is still an inferential overlay, not direct perturbation evidence.

The second paper is A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics. This is a strong reminder that many downstream network-neuromodulation claims rest on shaky source estimates. The paper uses patient-specific cortical eigenmodes as geometric basis functions for EEG and MEG source reconstruction and validates the idea across benchmarks, task data, resting-state networks, intracranial stimulation, and epilepsy settings. The useful read is that anatomy-constrained low-dimensional bases may be a better substrate for state estimation and targeting than generic smoothness priors.

The third paper is Bifurcation of neural firing patterns driven by potassium dynamics and neuron-electrode geometry during high-frequency stimulation. Using rat CA1 recordings plus a biophysically detailed multicompartment axon model, the authors argue that abrupt transitions between tonic, clustered, and low-rate firing during high-frequency stimulation depend jointly on electrode-axon geometry and peri-axonal potassium accumulation. That is mechanistically better than treating all high-frequency-stimulation effects as a simple conduction block. It is still a rodent hippocampal model rather than a direct DBS programming study, but it sharpens how we should think about state transitions under stimulation.

The fourth paper is Magnetic resonance identification tags for ultra-flexible electrodes. This is adjacent rather than immediately translational, but the problem is real: high-density flexible implants are hard to localize accurately after implantation. The authors build MRI-visible barcode-like tags into ultra-flexible electrode bundles and report around ninety-five-micron localization accuracy with stable chronic recordings in freely moving rats. The steal-worthy idea is not the specific hardware alone. It is the insistence that recording quality and anatomical identifiability have to travel together.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better neuromodulation thinking depends on three layers at once. First, you need a decent state-space story about which transitions are pathologically cheap or hard, not just which regions are correlated. Second, you need better measurement infrastructure, because whole-brain control rhetoric is weak if the inverse problem is crude. Third, you need more realistic stimulation physics and physiology, because abrupt response changes may come from geometry and extracellular chemistry together rather than a single cartoon mechanism. The common thread is simple: cleaner intervention logic needs cleaner latent-state models, cleaner observations, and cleaner mechanism stories.

digests.theme: Today is a state-aware stimulation logic, patient-specific network heterogeneity, and post-pulse network reconfiguration day. The most relevant paper is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity, because it makes a strong mechanistic point that stimulation effects depend not just on local phase but on the transient whole-network state the pulse lands in. The strongest translational-control paper is Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation, because it upgrades adaptive DBS from threshold folklore toward explicit state estimation while staying real-time feasible. The strongest personalized-modeling paper is Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration, because it treats VNS response heterogeneity as a model-identification problem rather than a vague clinical trait. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity. Using connectome-based whole-brain modeling, the authors ask how the impact of a single pulse depends on both local oscillatory phase and the current large-scale functional-connectivity configuration. The useful claim is not just that stimulation is state dependent, which is already familiar. The stronger claim is that network-aware state descriptors can improve prediction of stimulation effects by up to about forty percent and that pulses can trigger whole-brain state switching. That is exactly the kind of paper that sharpens intervention logic rather than merely decorating it.

The second paper is Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation. In chronic at-home recordings from three Parkinson's disease patients with sensing-enabled DBS systems, the authors compare instantaneous discriminant classifiers against hidden-Markov time-history models for classifying motor state from cortical entrained gamma and subthalamic beta biomarkers. The main result is modest but real: adding time history improves hyperkinetic-state detection and smooths predictions without sacrificing real-time feasibility. The limitation is obvious, namely the tiny sample, but the control framing is still better than most adaptive-DBS decoding papers.

The third paper is Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration. Using preimplant diffusion and functional MRI from thirty-eight children with drug-resistant epilepsy, the authors fit subject-specific reduced Wong-Wang whole-brain models and compare responders with nonresponders after VNS. Nonresponders show worse model-based predictability of functional connectivity, while responders show stronger inferred inhibitory weights in thalamic, cingulate, and frontal nodes of the vagal afferent network. This is still model-dependent association rather than proof of mechanism, but it is a serious attempt to make responder heterogeneity computationally legible.

The fourth paper is Intrinsic brain network dynamics modulated by neural stimulation to cerebellum. Here the authors use resting-state fMRI before and after inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to right cerebellar Crus I and analyze changes in dynamic community structure. Post stimulation, network flexibility rises and the dynamic patterns remain highly individual rather than collapsing into one canonical mode. This is not a clinical paper and not a targeting recipe, but it is useful for reminding us that stimulation can change large-scale integration and segregation properties in ways that simple average-connectivity summaries may miss.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better neuromodulation papers are getting more explicit about latent state. One paper says stimulation outcome depends on transient whole-network configuration, not just local phase. Another shows that adaptive DBS classifiers improve when they remember recent motor-state history instead of pretending each instant is independent. Another argues that VNS response heterogeneity may reflect whether a patient's network dynamics are even tractable to the intervention. And the cerebellar perturbation paper adds that stimulation can reshape modular flexibility in ways static summaries would hide. The common thread is simple: if you want better intervention logic, you need better state models.

digests.theme: Today is a generalization discipline, network-guided targeting, and control-side stimulation hygiene day. The most relevant paper is Complexity of resting cortical activity predicts neurophysiological responses to theta-burst stimulation but fails to generalize: A rigorous machine-learning approach, because it is one of the cleaner recent reminders that personalization claims in noninvasive neuromodulation often collapse when you demand external validation and test-retest realism. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Complexity of resting cortical activity predicts neurophysiological responses to theta-burst stimulation but fails to generalize: A rigorous machine-learning approach. The authors combine baseline resting-state EEG features with baseline transcranial magnetic stimulation measures to predict single-session intermittent theta-burst stimulation responses in two independent healthy-adult test-retest cohorts. Internal cross-validation looked promising, with about eighty-one percent binary accuracy, but external validation dropped to about sixty-nine percent. That is the useful result. The paper is valuable not because it found a magic predictor, but because it shows how easy it is to overread fragile personalization signals when stimulation effects themselves are unstable.

The second paper is Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Meige syndrome: mapping the optimal stimulation sites and network targets. In sixty-five patients across two centers, the authors combine local stimulation modeling with whole-brain functional-connectivity mapping and then validate the learned patterns in an independent cohort. The core claim is that best outcomes cluster in dorsolateral sensorimotor subthalamic nucleus extending toward associative territory, and at the network level align with positive connectivity to cerebellum and negative connectivity to somatosensory cortex. This is still normative-connectivity inference rather than direct mechanism, but it is a better targeting paper than most because it at least tries to survive external validation.

The third paper is Dithering suppresses half-harmonic neural synchronisation to photic stimulation in humans. Using EEG during periodic and jittered photic stimulation in healthy adults, the authors show that slightly jittering pulse timing suppresses half-harmonic synchronisation more than it suppresses synchronisation at the target frequency. The main value is conceptual. If periodic stimulation can create unwanted subharmonic or superharmonic locking, then control policies should care not only about how much energy is delivered, but about the temporal regularity of delivery.

The fourth paper is Piezoelectric neuromodulation of the subthalamic nucleus ameliorates motor and nonmotor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. In a six-hydroxydopamine mouse model, ultrasound-responsive nanoparticles injected into subthalamic nucleus were used to drive repeated deep-target stimulation, with reported improvements in gait, pain, anxiety-like behavior, and nigrostriatal pathology. This is worth keeping as interface-design inspiration, but the translational pitch should be kept on a short leash. Intracranial particle injection plus ultrasound actuation is not a clean substitute for conventional deep brain stimulation, and the abstract alone does not prove precise, state-specific neuromodulation.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better neuromodulation work gets stricter about hidden failure modes. The computational paper says personalization models break when stimulation effects are not themselves stable. The Meige study says targeting claims are more believable when they survive independent validation and link local anatomy to a distributed network. The dithering paper says periodic stimulation can create unwanted structure that should be engineered away rather than ignored. And the nanoparticle paper is a reminder that novel actuation hardware is not the same thing as demonstrated therapeutic control.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-03
digests.theme: Today is a targeting realism, state-dependent network coupling, and heterogeneity-mapping day. The most relevant paper is Varying patterns of association between cortical large-scale networks and subthalamic nucleus activity in Parkinson's disease, because it links dynamic cortical network states to subthalamic activity in a way that could matter for closed-loop deep brain stimulation rather than just for descriptive Parkinson's physiology. The strongest translational targeting paper is Bayesian probabilistic density mapping of the decussating dentato-rubro-thalamic tract to predict clinical tremor improvement in MRgFUS, because it argues that the tract people usually do not visualize may be closer to the real therapeutic pathway than the usual indirect coordinate logic. The most practically important methods paper is Robustness of lead reconstruction for deep brain stimulation modelling and probabilistic mapping, because it tests how stable the computational geometry is before people build sweet-spot maps and automated programming logic on top of it. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Varying patterns of association between cortical large-scale networks and subthalamic nucleus activity in Parkinson's disease. Using simultaneous magnetoencephalography and subthalamic local field potentials from twenty-seven Parkinson's patients on and off dopaminergic medication, the authors fit a time-delay embedded hidden Markov model to identify recurring cortical network states and then ask how each state relates to subthalamic activity. The useful result is not just that subthalamic beta matters. It is that subthalamic-supplementary-motor-area synchrony depends on which cortical network is active, with different frequency structure in sensorimotor versus posterior default-mode states. That is exactly the kind of state-conditional coupling logic that closed-loop stimulation systems should care about.

The second paper is Bayesian probabilistic density mapping of the decussating dentato-rubro-thalamic tract to predict clinical tremor improvement in MRgFUS. In twenty-eight patients undergoing unilateral MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy for essential tremor, the authors use Bayesian diffusion modeling and probabilistic tractography to compare three targeting references: the classic indirect coordinate, the nondecussating dentato-rubro-thalamic tract, and the decussating dentato-rubro-thalamic tract. In the subgroup with adequate lesion temperature, distance from lesion to the decussating tract correlated most strongly with clinical improvement. The paper does not solve targeting, but it does say that conventional tract assumptions may be pointed at the wrong fiber population.

The third paper is Robustness of lead reconstruction for deep brain stimulation modelling and probabilistic mapping. In thirty-four deep brain stimulation patients who each had two postoperative CT scans, the authors process each scan independently through Lead-DBS and compare lead-tip coordinates, volumes of tissue activation, and group-level probabilistic maps. The reassuring part is that group-level probabilistic maps stay fairly robust. The uncomfortable part is that individual-level volume-of-tissue-activation overlap is materially variable, especially at lower amplitudes. That means sweet-spot mapping may survive current reconstruction error better than individualized programming logic does.

The fourth paper is Parsing neurobiological heterogeneity in treatment-resistant depression using brain network localization. This is a meta-analytic-plus-network-mapping paper that combines reported neuroimaging abnormalities with large normative resting-state functional MRI datasets to derive network patterns for treatment-resistant depression versus controls, non-treatment-resistant depression versus controls, and treatment-resistant versus non-treatment-resistant depression. The main value is organizational: it suggests that treatment-resistant depression may concentrate more strongly in ventral attention and default-network circuitry than non-treatment-resistant depression. That is not yet causal targeting logic, but it is more useful than treating treatment resistance as one undifferentiated imaging blob.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that targeting and control get better only when the hidden geometry and hidden state structure become explicit. The Parkinson's MEG plus subthalamic paper says biomarkers live inside changing cortical network states. The focused-ultrasound tractography paper says your lesion may only work when it lands near the right crossing fiber bundle. The lead-reconstruction paper says individualized modeling error is still large enough to matter even if group maps look stable. And the treatment-resistant depression mapping paper is a reminder that heterogeneity work is only valuable when it sharpens circuits and targets instead of adding another layer of descriptive fog.

The most ambitious computational paper is Inverting Foundation Models of Brain Function with Simulation-Based Inference, because it tries to turn whole-brain emulators into inverse-design tools instead of just predictive toys. The flashiest translational paper is Piezoelectric neuromodulation of the subthalamic nucleus ameliorates motor and nonmotor symptoms of Parkinson's disease, but it is more an intriguing device-direction paper than near-term intervention evidence.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Spatial Effects of Electrode Configurations and Source Depth in EEG Source Localization: Implications for Concurrent Noninvasive Brain Stimulation with HD-EEG. Using simultaneous stereoelectroencephalography and two-hundred-fifty-six-channel high-density EEG from seven epilepsy patients with single-pulse intracranial stimulation as ground truth, the authors test what happens when electrodes near or far from the source are removed or interpolated. The result is pleasantly concrete: degradation near the source hurts localization substantially, distal degradation barely matters, and sparse or parametric inverse methods like MxNE, dipole fitting, and RAP-MUSIC are more resilient than common distributed methods. That is exactly the kind of boring but high-leverage constraint that should shape any concurrent stimulation-plus-EEG protocol.

The second paper is Dynamic causal modeling of effective connectivity generating a reduced auditory deviance detection in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. In sixty people with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and thirty-nine controls, the authors combine a roving auditory oddball task, two-hundred-fifty-six-channel EEG, dynamic causal modeling, and Parametric Empirical Bayes. The headline is not just smaller mismatch-negativity and P3a responses. It is a more specific network claim: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy shows reduced right superior-temporal to right inferior-frontal feedforward connectivity during deviance processing, plus increased intrinsic excitability in left superior temporal gyrus. That is more useful than saying epilepsy patients have altered cognition, because it points toward a tractable circuit-level deficit model.

The third paper is Inverting Foundation Models of Brain Function with Simulation-Based Inference. This arXiv preprint uses the TRIBEv2 brain-activity foundation model plus large language model-generated stimuli to ask whether synthetic brain maps can be inverted back to latent stimulus properties like valence, arousal, and dominance. It is still proof-of-concept work and not a neuromodulation paper. But it matters because it reframes whole-brain models as controllable experimental objects: instead of only predicting responses to given stimuli, the model is used to infer what kind of stimulus would produce a desired neural pattern. The idea is strategically important even if the present demo is still toy-sized.

The fourth paper is Piezoelectric neuromodulation of the subthalamic nucleus ameliorates motor and nonmotor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. In a six-hydroxydopamine mouse model, ultrasound-responsive piezoelectric nanoparticles were injected into subthalamic nucleus and then driven wirelessly with ultrasound over several days. The authors report improvement in gait, pain, anxiety-like phenotypes, dopaminergic preservation, and reduced neuroinflammatory and mitochondrial pathology. The interesting part is not the disease-overclaim. It is the attempt to approximate deep-target stimulation without conventional implanted leads. Still, this remains invasive in a different way, biologically early, and far from proving a clinically credible replacement for deep brain stimulation.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that intervention logic only gets stronger when the measurement layer, the mechanistic layer, and the generative-model layer all become less hand-wavy. The HD-EEG source-localization paper says practical sensor geometry matters more than people like to admit. The juvenile myoclonic epilepsy paper gives a cleaner directional-connectivity account of deviance-processing impairment. The foundation-model inversion preprint hints at a future where simulated brain models are used for inverse design, not just forward prediction. And the piezoelectric subthalamic paper is a reminder that new actuation hardware is only interesting if it eventually meets the same mechanistic and translational standards as old hardware.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-05-01
digests.theme: Today is a personalization skepticism, state-geometry, and timing day. The most relevant paper is Differential effects of individualized vs. fixed-frequency tACS on clinical and EEG outcomes in major depressive disorder, because it tests a personalization story that a lot of noninvasive stimulation papers assume rather than earn. The strongest network paper is Hippocampal-parietal directed connectivity mediates brain network reconfiguration between internal and external attention: An intracranial EEG study, because it gives a cleaner effective-connectivity account of state switching than the usual static-attention-network talk. The strongest methods paper is MapperEEG: A topological approach to brain state clustering in EEG recordings, because state clustering is upstream of many adaptive-control claims and this paper actually benchmarks against reasonable alternatives. The most conceptually useful preclinical stimulation paper is Micro-Stimulation Timing Framed Around an Averaged Theta Period of Stimulation Determines Hippocampal Recruitment in Cued Fear Conditioning, because it treats stimulation timing as a structured code rather than just a pulse count.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Differential effects of individualized vs. fixed-frequency tACS on clinical and EEG outcomes in major depressive disorder. In a randomized double-blind trial, seventy-two outpatients with major depressive disorder were assigned to fixed ten-hertz versus individualized-alpha-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation, each delivered either once or twice daily over twenty sessions. The clinically important result is not a personalization win. There was no significant efficacy advantage for individualized-alpha stimulation over fixed-frequency stimulation, and no clean administration-frequency effect either. The useful residue is narrower: fixed-frequency and higher-administration arms showed trend-level symptom improvement, while EEG measures suggested protocol-dependent modulation of frontal connectivity and parietal alpha power. That makes this more useful as a brake on casual IAF personalization rhetoric than as a success story.

The second paper is Hippocampal-parietal directed connectivity mediates brain network reconfiguration between internal and external attention: An intracranial EEG study. Using stereo-EEG from seventeen patients with refractory epilepsy performing a sustained-attention task, the authors built directed effective-connectivity graphs with high-frequency broadband activity and Granger causality. External attention was associated with stronger global causal connectivity and more connector-hub structure, while internal attention showed higher modularity and more peripheral-node organization. The most interesting mechanistic point is that hippocampal self-dynamics and hippocampal outflow to middle temporal gyrus were among the most discriminative features, which is a more memory-linked account of attentional state switching than generic frontoparietal slogans.

The third paper is MapperEEG: A topological approach to brain state clustering in EEG recordings. This is not a clinical neuromodulation paper, but it matters because a lot of adaptive-stimulation and biomarker work quietly assumes that brain states can be clustered cleanly. MapperEEG combines classical EEG features with topological Mapper graphs to cluster states in spectral space and represent their connectivity, then compares against six other clustering approaches including hierarchical clustering, hidden Markov models, and basic autoencoders. The authors report better state identification in a tapping task and useful structural readouts even when clustering is otherwise messy. If that holds up, it is a potentially practical upgrade for state discovery rather than another vague topology-for-brains performance piece.

The fourth paper is Micro-Stimulation Timing Framed Around an Averaged Theta Period of Stimulation Determines Hippocampal Recruitment in Cued Fear Conditioning. In mice, the authors delivered six-pulse microstimulation patterns across a one-hundred-forty-millisecond theta cycle in CA3 during auditory fear conditioning, comparing a fixed temporal pattern against randomized timing and sham. Only the fixed-pattern stimulation increased freezing relative to sham and produced stronger hippocampal c-Fos recruitment after retrieval. The useful lesson is not that this is ready for translation. It is that temporal packaging itself can act like a control variable, which matters for any stimulation program that claims phase sensitivity without specifying what temporal code is actually being imposed.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that better intervention logic needs stronger discipline about what counts as personalization, what counts as a brain state, and what counts as timing. The tACS trial says individualized alpha frequency is not yet an earned antidepressant targeting principle. The intracranial attention paper sharpens the state-transition story with directed hippocampal-temporal-parietal interactions rather than just broad resting-state labels. MapperEEG matters because if state clustering is weak, then closed-loop rhetoric built on those states is fragile. And the hippocampal microstimulation paper is a reminder that temporal structure itself may be part of the intervention, not just the carrier for it.
