digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-30
digests.theme: Today is a targeting-and-measurement honesty day. The most relevant paper is Target engagement in a head-to-head clinical trial of dysphoric versus anxiosomatic transcranial magnetic stimulation targets, because it tests a claim many circuit-TMS papers glide past: whether different symptom-targeted sites actually engage distinct circuits in a clinically meaningful way. The strongest translational network paper is Temporal Interference Stimulation Modulates Resting State Functional Connectivity of Motor Circuit in Parkinson's Disease, because it gives early human imaging evidence that subthalamic temporal-interference stimulation may shift the expected motor-circuit edges, even if the study is still small and acute. The strongest methods and computational paper is A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics, because better source reconstruction is upstream of a lot of flashy network-control rhetoric. The most practical signal-processing paper is Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending, because TMS-EEG remains half theater if artifact cleanup fails exactly when the data get ugly.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Target engagement in a head-to-head clinical trial of dysphoric versus anxiosomatic transcranial magnetic stimulation targets. In a modest randomized trial, patients with depression and anxiety received thirty TMS sessions at either a dorsolateral prefrontal target intended to affect dysphoric symptoms or a dorsomedial prefrontal target intended to affect anxiosomatic symptoms. The sharp result is not a triumphant personalization win. It is more awkward and therefore more useful: post-treatment connectivity change was not clearly target-specific and did not predict symptom improvement, while baseline connectivity from the stimulation site to the intended circuit did predict circuit change and anxiety improvement, mainly in the anxiosomatic arm. That is a better targeting lesson than another victory-lap abstract.

The second paper is Temporal Interference Stimulation Modulates Resting State Functional Connectivity of Motor Circuit in Parkinson's Disease. In a randomized double-blind crossover design, twenty-three patients with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease underwent a single twenty-minute 130 hertz temporal-interference session aimed at the subthalamic nucleus versus active sham, with pre and post resting-state functional MRI. The reported pattern, decreased connectivity between the targeted subthalamic nucleus and striatum but increased connectivity with primary motor cortex, is plausible enough to take seriously as a mechanistic clue. The main limitation is that this is still an acute imaging study with no strong symptom mediation story.

The third paper is A geometry aware framework enhances noninvasive mapping of whole human brain dynamics. This is not itself a neuromodulation trial, but it may matter more than a lot of weak personalization papers because it attacks the inverse problem directly. The authors use patient-specific geometric basis functions derived from cortical surface eigenmodes as anatomical priors for EEG and MEG source reconstruction, then validate the approach across benchmarks, task data, resting-state networks, intracranial stimulation, and epilepsy cases. If that holds up, it improves the quality of the whole-brain dynamical maps that many targeting and control claims quietly depend on.

The fourth paper is Effective correction of extreme capacitive artifacts in TMS-EEG via windowed detrending. The paper compares standard detrending and ICA-heavy cleanup against a windowed approach that separately models artifact charging and discharging phases. The interesting part is not that one more denoising method exists. It is that ICA breaks down when capacitive artifacts become severe, whereas windowed detrending seems more robust across hardware setups and artifact intensities. That matters because a lot of TMS-EEG interpretation fails precisely in the messy cases.
digests.takeaway: The real pattern today is that better neuromodulation requires more honesty about what has actually been engaged and measured. The head-to-head TMS paper suggests that baseline circuit architecture may be a better biomarker than pre-post connectivity theater. The temporal-interference Parkinson paper is interesting because it moves from pure concept toward human circuit readouts, but it is still preliminary. The geometry-aware source-imaging paper improves the measurement substrate underneath network-control claims. And the TMS-EEG artifact paper shows, again, that bad measurements quietly poison a lot of higher-level interpretation. The common theme is simple: targeting logic is only as good as the state and circuit estimates underneath it.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-29
digests.theme: Today is an adaptive-control and dynamic-network-biomarker day. The most relevant paper is Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation, because it tests a simple but actually useful idea for closed-loop DBS: stop classifying motor state from single noisy moments and add temporal state history explicitly. The strongest clinical-network paper is Predicting rTMS treatment efficacy in depression based on modular flexibility of functional connectivity, because it ties symptom change to a dynamic network quantity rather than to static connectivity slogans, even if the sample is still modest and retrospective. The strongest methods paper is Efficient artifact removal for adaptive deep brain stimulation and a temporal event localization analysis, because real-time closed-loop systems live or die on whether the sensed signal is usable during stimulation. The best broader computational paper is Personalized whole-brain Ising models with heterogeneous nodes capture differences among brain regions, which is not a neuromodulation paper per se but is worth keeping because it sharpens how individualized whole-brain models might represent region-level heterogeneity instead of pretending every node is the same.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation. Using chronic at-home recordings from three Parkinson's disease patients with sensing-enabled implants, the authors compare instantaneous classifiers against hidden-Markov time-history models for classifying hypokinetic versus hyperkinetic states. The useful result is not just a small accuracy bump. It is that adding temporal structure materially improves hyperkinetic-state detection while keeping latency and compute low enough for real-time deployment. That is exactly the kind of boring-but-important systems improvement adaptive DBS needs.

The second paper is Predicting rTMS treatment efficacy in depression based on modular flexibility of functional connectivity. In seventy patients with major depressive disorder receiving active or sham rTMS, the authors claim that active treatment increases medial prefrontal default-mode flexibility and that baseline default-mode flexibility predicts post-treatment symptom burden. The framing is better than most biomarker papers because the proposed mechanism is dynamic network adaptability rather than a static connectivity fetish. The caveat is that the evidence is still retrospective, the prediction effect is moderate, and the individualized targeting story rests on nucleus-accumbens connectivity without especially strong causal proof.

The third paper is Efficient artifact removal for adaptive deep brain stimulation and a temporal event localization analysis. SMARTA+ extends prior back-end artifact removal so that stimulation artifacts and transient direct-current artifacts can be suppressed with much lower computational cost. In semi-real and patient Parkinson data, the method preserves local field potential structure and improves beta-burst event localization relative to simpler blanking and subtraction baselines. This is not glamorous, but it is crucial. If the sensed signal is distorted, the rest of the closed-loop stack is theater.

The fourth paper is Personalized whole-brain Ising models with heterogeneous nodes capture differences among brain regions. This is the least directly interventional paper in today's set, but it is still worth preserving because it pushes whole-brain modeling away from homogeneous-node simplifications and toward personalized, structurally anchored heterogeneity. The authors fit 360-region Ising models with GPU-accelerated Boltzmann learning, study threshold effects, and relate node parameters to structural features like myelination and cortical folding. It is not yet a control paper, but it is potentially useful infrastructure for future intervention-relevant digital-twin work.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that adaptive neuromodulation gets stronger when papers take dynamics seriously at multiple levels. The Bayesian aDBS paper models temporal continuity in motor state instead of trusting noisy moment-to-moment thresholds. The rTMS depression paper treats response as a problem of network flexibility rather than static connectivity snapshots. SMARTA+ deals with the unglamorous but essential fact that sensing during stimulation is messy, and the whole-brain Ising paper pushes personalized modeling toward richer node-level heterogeneity. None of these papers solves precision neuromodulation. But together they make the intervention stack, state estimation, network interpretation, and modeling substrate a bit more honest.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-28
digests.theme: Today is a state-aware targeting and control-geometry day. The most relevant paper is Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus, because it actually uses a patient-specific whole-brain model to ask which targets move which abnormal state instead of treating target choice as sloganized location picking. The strongest network-control paper is Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals, because it makes stimulation geometry more realistic and shows that diffuse control can reduce transition energy dramatically. The clearest clinical adaptive paper is Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome, which is still only a case study but at least ties adaptation to a real biomarker and a real operational use case. The best methods paper is Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study, because it makes the usual personalization problem painfully concrete across nearly six hundred aging-brain anatomies.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus. The authors built a tinnitus-specific digital twin brain from multimodal imaging and used more than 1.64 million virtual stimulations to map how different targets shift two abnormal whole-brain states, one more sensory-weighted and one more cognitive-default-mode weighted. The useful claim is not that tinnitus targeting is solved. The useful claim is that state-specific target choice may be the right abstraction, and the authors do at least validate their response maps against an independent repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation dataset.

The second paper is Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals. This is not a clinical trial. It is a network-control paper arguing that the usual node-by-node control assumption is physically silly for cortex and for real stimulation devices. When the authors allow inputs to spread spatially with exponential decay, state transitions require much less energy and can often be approximated with far fewer input sites. That matters because intervention logic should respect the fact that stimulation is not a perfectly local delta function.

The third paper is Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome. In one patient with refractory Tourette syndrome and obsessive-compulsive disorder, chronic sensing from ventral capsule or ventral striatum and centromedian-parafascicular thalamus showed circadian beta rhythms that were then used to reduce stimulation automatically during sleep. The result is still fragile single-patient evidence, but it is a respectable proof of concept for slow adaptive control driven by a clinically usable day-night signal rather than by fragile moment-to-moment detection.

The fourth paper is Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study. Using finite-element simulations in 590 Human Connectome Project-Aging participants, the authors show that montage, skull thickness, cerebrospinal-fluid thickness, cortical thickness, local gyrification, and sulcal depth all materially shift where current actually goes. The important read is not that one montage wins universally. It is that standardized dosing still produces highly nonstandardized electric fields.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that neuromodulation gets better when papers stop pretending stimulation is either perfectly local or perfectly generic. The tinnitus digital-twin study asks which target changes which abnormal state. The diffuse-input control paper shows that realistic spatial spread changes the control problem itself. The Tourette adaptive DBS case uses a slow, interpretable biomarker tied to actual sleep-wake needs instead of chasing flashy millisecond adaptivity. And the tDCS montage paper reminds us that anatomy still decides a lot of what the protocol really is. Taken together, this is a good day for state-aware and geometry-aware intervention logic.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-27
digests.theme: Today is a personalization and controllable-state day. The most relevant paper is Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration, because it ties VNS outcome heterogeneity to patient-specific biophysical brain models instead of leaving response as clinical fog. The strongest targeting paper is Reduced pre-treatment isolated effective coherence between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex as a potential predictive marker for remission following repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in major depressive disorder, because it asks for a directional circuit marker rather than another vague connectivity slogan. The clearest control paper is Brain-computer interface-based neurofeedback training enables transferable control of cortical state switching in humans, because it shows that people can be trained to reshape cortical transition dynamics and carry that control outside the training interface. The clinical paper is Bilateral DLPFC Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation for Mood and Motor Symptoms in Parkinson's Disease: A Preliminary Study, which is interesting mainly as an apathy-linked proof of concept rather than as definitive motor evidence.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration. The authors built individualized reduced Wong-Wang virtual brains from preimplant diffusion and functional MRI in thirty-eight children with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing VNS. Model fit to empirical functional connectivity was worse in nonresponders, and responders showed stronger inferred inhibitory weights in parts of the vagal afferent network, including thalamic, cingulate, and frontal regions. The useful read is that VNS response may depend on whether a patient’s network can be captured by a relatively coherent mesoscopic dynamical model, not just on seizure labels or demographics. The caveat is that the sample is still small, outcome is responder status rather than richer longitudinal control, and the inferred inhibitory parameters are model-dependent.

The second paper is Reduced pre-treatment isolated effective coherence between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex as a potential predictive marker for remission following repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in major depressive disorder. In thirty adults with major depressive disorder treated with high-frequency left DLPFC rTMS, lower baseline alpha-band directed connectivity from left DLPFC to sgACC was associated with remission, with an area under the curve of 0.75 and an odds ratio of 0.25 in multivariable analysis. This is not enough to call it a deployable biomarker, but it is better than generic correlation worship because it tests a directional pre-treatment circuit quantity tied to a real treatment question.

The third paper is Brain-computer interface-based neurofeedback training enables transferable control of cortical state switching in humans. The main claim is that real-time neurofeedback can train people to deliberately modulate sensorimotor state transitions, and that the learned control generalizes beyond the explicit BCI setting. Data-driven latent-state analysis linked successful control to stronger interregional phase coupling and steeper broadband spectral slope in medial frontal cortex, alongside faster muscle contraction and relaxation reaction times. This matters because it treats brain-state control as something trainable and transferable, not just measurable after the fact.

The fourth paper is Bilateral DLPFC Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation for Mood and Motor Symptoms in Parkinson's Disease: A Preliminary Study. Patients with Parkinson’s disease and mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms received ten bilateral DLPFC tDCS sessions, and the authors report improvements in mood, anxiety, apathy, motor ratings, quality of life, and daily step count. The interesting part is the apathy and behavior angle, not the strength of the efficacy claim. Without a sham arm, this is still soft clinical evidence.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that neuromodulation gets more interesting when papers stop treating response as a black box. The pediatric VNS study tries to model response heterogeneity with patient-specific dynamical brains. The rTMS paper asks whether directional DLPFC to sgACC coupling can separate remitters from nonremitters before treatment. The neurofeedback paper shows that cortical state switching is not just a descriptive latent story but something humans may learn to control. And the Parkinson tDCS paper is worth keeping mainly because it hints that apathy-linked motivational circuitry may sit closer to functional benefit than another narrow motor-score narrative.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-26
digests.theme: Today is a causal perturbation and control-logic day. The most relevant paper is Transcranial temporal interference stimulation targeting the subthalamic region for motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease: a pilot, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover study, because it is one of the rare temporal-interference papers that actually forces the technique to answer a clinical question under blinded conditions instead of hiding behind field-model aesthetics. The best computational-control paper is Quantifying State-Dependent Control Properties of Brain Dynamics from Perturbation Responses, because it moves network control theory closer to system identification by estimating control properties from actual perturbation responses instead of resting-state fantasy. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Transcranial temporal interference stimulation targeting the subthalamic region for motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease: a pilot, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover study. In thirty people with early-to-mid-stage Parkinson's disease, a single twenty-minute individualized temporal-interference session targeting the subthalamic region improved medication-off motor scores versus sham at immediate, thirty-minute, and sixty-minute follow-up, with a 70 percent responder rate against 15 percent for sham. That is stronger than the usual temporal-interference literature, which often asks for mechanistic admiration before showing meaningful human effect. The caveat is that this is still a small short-term crossover study, so durability, anatomical specificity, and reproducibility remain unsettled.

The second paper is Non-vectorial integration of intersectional short-pulse stimulation enables enhanced deep brain modulation and effective seizure control. The paper argues that rapidly switched pulse trains can sum at the membrane level in a way that improves deep modulation without relying on classical extracellular field-vector addition. The authors support that claim with finite-element modeling, cadaver measurements, whole-cell patch clamp, and closed-loop seizure experiments in a rat kindling model, where intersectional short-pulse stimulation reduced seizure duration and severity more than conventional transcranial electrical stimulation. The reason to keep it is that it is an unusually complete stack from biophysics to function. The reason not to overclaim is that rodent seizure control is not yet human therapeutic proof.

The third paper is Quantifying State-Dependent Control Properties of Brain Dynamics from Perturbation Responses. This paper takes a good swing at a real weakness in control-style brain modeling. Rather than inferring controllability from unperturbed data alone, it estimates a controllability Gramian directly from single-trial TMS-EEG responses and uses the eigenstructure of that Gramian to compare intrinsic control properties across resting, motor-imagery, and motor-execution states. The useful part is not the six-class decoding result by itself. The useful part is the methodological claim that perturbation responses can identify which state dimensions are actually easier or harder to steer.

The fourth paper is Frontal connectivity dynamics encode contextual information during action preparation. Using TMS-EEG during Go and No-Go tasks with different target probabilities, the authors show that alpha-band right inferior frontal gyrus connectivity and beta-band frontal connectivity track proactive inhibition and contextual action likelihood before a movement even happens. This matters because it treats cognition as time-varying interareal control rather than just local activation in a favorite region. It is not a stimulation paper, but it is exactly the kind of causal systems result that sharpens intervention logic.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that neurostimulation gets more credible when it is forced to meet perturbation logic all the way down. The Parkinson temporal-interference trial matters because it at least tests whether a fashionable noninvasive deep-targeting idea buys measurable symptom change under sham control. The intersectional short-pulse paper matters because it gives a specific membrane-integration story and then checks whether that story actually improves seizure control. The controllability paper matters because it treats stimulation responses as system-identification data rather than decorative perturbations. And the frontal-connectivity paper matters because it shows the kind of dynamic network variable that future interventions may need to read or steer.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-25
digests.theme: Today is a state-logic and intervention-credibility day. The most relevant paper is Neuromodulation-induced normalization of cortical metastable dynamics signatures in Parkinson's disease, because it tries to connect symptom relief across invasive and noninvasive subthalamic stimulation to a shared whole-brain state signature instead of stopping at local target mythology. The strongest developmental psychiatry paper is Graph theory reveals functional connectome disruptions in adolescent major depressive disorder with childhood trauma, because it combines a large adolescent cohort with longitudinal imaging and at least attempts response prediction from baseline network structure. The best computational framing paper is Brain energetic landscapes shape state dysregulation in major depressive disorder: a morphological network controllability perspective, because it turns depressive state instability into an energy-budget question rather than another static-connectivity list. The cleanest clinical anchor is Postapproval Study for Brain-Responsive Neurostimulation for Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy: Three-Year Efficacy and Interim Safety Results, because it is not flashy but it does show what durable real-world responsive stimulation evidence actually looks like.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Neuromodulation-induced normalization of cortical metastable dynamics signatures in Parkinson's disease. The authors use resting-state functional MRI and a new Weighted Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis, or WEiDA, to identify recurring probabilistic metastable substates in Parkinson's disease. Their headline claim is that subthalamic deep brain stimulation restores occupancy of a specific cortical state involving decoupling between visual and somatomotor-ventral-attention systems, and that a similar normalization appears during subthalamic-targeted transcranial temporal interference stimulation. The attractive part is the shared state-space framing across invasive and noninvasive modalities. The caveat is that the noninvasive arm risks being read as stronger mechanistic confirmation than abstract-level evidence really supports.

The second paper is Graph theory reveals functional connectome disruptions in adolescent major depressive disorder with childhood trauma. This is a larger and more clinically serious adolescent depression dataset than most papers in this lane: 343 adolescents with depression and 149 healthy controls, with a childhood-trauma stratification and longitudinal follow-up. The authors report greater network randomness, deficits in default-mode hubs, post-treatment normalization in the precuneus and amygdala, and baseline-connectome prediction of antidepressant response at 82 percent accuracy. The useful part is the trauma-stratified network logic and the longitudinal design. The weak part is the usual risk that a decent discrimination number gets overpromoted as a clinically actionable biomarker before site robustness is shown.

The third paper is Brain energetic landscapes shape state dysregulation in major depressive disorder: a morphological network controllability perspective. This paper argues that major depression involves reduced dynamic stability, too many within-state transitions, too few between-state transitions, and impaired control energy centered in default-mode and limbic nodes such as posterior cingulate cortex and temporal pole. The reason to keep it is not that morphological network controllability is automatically trustworthy. The reason is that it links brain-state dysregulation to energy constraints across imaging, metabolic, and cellular layers, which is closer to an intervention-relevant control story than generic graph metrics. Still, this remains an inference-heavy paper, and the path from energy-vulnerable nodes to actual stimulation targets is not solved.

The fourth paper is Postapproval Study for Brain-Responsive Neurostimulation for Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy: Three-Year Efficacy and Interim Safety Results. This is not conceptually sexy, but it is exactly the sort of real-world benchmark the field needs. In 324 implanted patients across 32 US centers, median seizure reduction reached 82 percent at three years, 41 percent achieved at least 90 percent seizure reduction, and no serious stimulation-related adverse events were reported. It matters because it shows what a mature adaptive-stimulation evidence base looks like when the claim is durable clinical effect rather than just an appealing control diagram.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that intervention logic gets better when it is framed in terms of states, transitions, and credible control constraints, but it only earns trust when there is real longitudinal or multicenter evidence behind it. The Parkinson metastability paper is the most interesting because it tries to map symptom relief onto restoration of a specific brain-state distribution across modalities. The adolescent trauma paper matters because it treats heterogeneity as central rather than annoying. The controllability paper matters because it gives depression a transition-energy framing that could someday inform targeting. And the RNS study matters because it anchors all of this in the reality that durable clinical neuromodulation is hard and has to prove itself over years, not diagrams.

digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Automating Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation Programming with Evoked Resonant Neural Activity in Parkinson's Disease. In twelve Parkinson's patients with well-placed subthalamic leads, an automated programming rule based on intraoperative evoked resonant neural activity, or ERNA, produced acute motor benefit and side-effect thresholds similar to expert clinician programming and imaging-guided programming. The useful point is not that programming is solved. It is that a sub-minute physiological readout may be good enough to give clinicians an objective starting point instead of a slow heuristic search.

The second paper is Cortical vs Subcortical Recordings to Drive Closed-Loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Essential Tremor. This is a small four-patient implanted study, but it asks the right question. If you want movement-linked closed-loop control in essential tremor, should the biomarker come from the thalamus near stimulation, or from sensorimotor cortex via a separate cortical strip? The authors report that cortical sensing performs better and remains more stable over time, with months of home use. That is valuable because it treats adaptive stimulation as a measurement-design problem, not just a threshold-tuning problem.

The third paper is TuneS: Patient-specific model-based optimization of contact configuration in deep brain stimulation. This is a ten-patient Parkinson's disease methods paper rather than outcome proof, but it is strong on intervention logic. TuneS combines patient-specific stimulation-spread models with predefined targets and avoidance constraints, including streamline targets, to predict contact configurations that improve target coverage while reducing stimulation of regions associated with side effects. That is more useful than treating programming as a black box or claiming connectomic personalization without an explicit optimization objective.

The fourth paper is Limitations of Variational Laplace-Based Dynamic Causal Modelling for Multistable Cortical Circuits. It is not a neuromodulation trial, but it matters for the mechanistic layer underneath many network-targeting and state-estimation papers. In simulated cortical circuits with bistability, period-doubling, and chaos, dynamic causal modelling could often identify the correct architecture yet still recover wrong extrinsic parameters and wrong reconstructed dynamics. The warning is simple: a clean effective-connectivity story can still be dynamically false.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that credible personalization needs an objective measurement or optimization layer. ERNA-guided programming matters because it gives DBS programming a fast physiological anchor. The essential-tremor closed-loop paper matters because it compares candidate sensing substrates in real use and finds that cortical signals may travel better over time than local subcortical ones. TuneS matters because it turns target coverage and avoidance into an explicit optimization problem. And the DCM paper matters because mechanistic inference can fail even when the model-selection output looks reassuring. If the sensing or inference layer is weak, the personalization story is usually theater.

The most relevant paper today is Residential Therapy With Navigated Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Combat-Related PTSD. This is a randomized sham-controlled trial in one hundred nineteen military personnel within an intensive residential PTSD program. Both groups improved, which is what you would expect inside a strong residential package, but active navigated TMS still produced additional symptom benefit and better durability on some follow-up measures. The useful part is not just that TMS helped. It is that the targeting was individualized anatomically and connectomically, then delivered with robotic stereotaxy inside a real treatment stack.

The second paper is StimVision: smartphone video kinematics to optimize DBS programming in Parkinson’s disease. This is a small fifteen-patient study, but the logic is excellent. Instead of relying on clinician impression alone, it extracts twenty-three markerless kinematic features from standard smartphone video and uses a patient-specific weighted score to rank stimulation programs. That is exactly the kind of cheap instrumentation layer that could make programming more reproducible without requiring an exotic sensing stack.

The third paper is Gamma Oscillations in Basolateral Amygdala as a Mechanistic and Predictive Biomarker for Prefrontal DBS Analgesia. This is a rat pain-model study rather than a clinical paper, but it is strong on intervention logic. The authors vary prefrontal DBS parameters while recording basolateral amygdala local field potentials and show that effective analgesia is associated with enhanced ongoing fast gamma, reduced nociceptive gamma, and a baseline oscillatory state that helps predict response. That is a much more useful closed-loop story than vague talk about network modulation.

The fourth paper is Connection density affects the behavior of functional brain network metrics. This is not a stimulation paper, but it is worth keeping because it explains why many patient-versus-control network claims are so unstable. Across Alzheimer disease, mild cognitive impairment, and schizophrenia datasets, the sign of group differences in common network metrics can reverse as connection density changes. That does not make network neuroscience worthless. It means a lot of published metric rhetoric is less robust than it sounds.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that good intervention papers increasingly need a credible measurement layer. The PTSD trial matters because it embeds individualized targeting in a proper sham-controlled treatment context. StimVision matters because it turns routine video into a programmable outcome surface for DBS. The basolateral-amygdala gamma paper matters because it treats efficacy as a state-dependent control problem rather than a binary stimulation label. And the connection-density paper matters because it warns that many network summaries are more fragile than the field admits. If the measurement layer is weak, the personalization story is usually weaker than advertised.

The most relevant paper today is Temporal interference stimulation (TIS) for major depressive disorder: right lingual gyrus as a predictor. This is a multicenter randomized double-blind sham-controlled trial with seventy-six major-depression patients, framed as a secondary analysis of right-amygdala-targeted temporal interference stimulation. The useful part is not the usual deep-stimulation branding. It is the attempt to identify a baseline imaging feature, lower right lingual-gyrus ALFF, that predicts who benefits. That is still a modest biomarker story rather than a mature precision-therapy result, but it is better than pretending the target alone settles the problem.

The second paper is Utilizing stimulation-evoked hemodynamic activity to predict antidepressant response to intermittent theta-burst stimulation in adults with major depression. This is a smaller study, forty-four patients plus healthy controls, but the logic is more mechanistically appealing than many response-prediction papers. Instead of asking only who looks depressed at baseline, it measures prefrontal hemodynamic response during concurrent theta-burst stimulation and functional near-infrared spectroscopy, then uses that evoked response to predict four-week treatment outcome. The support-vector-machine result looks good on paper, but the reliability spread is wide enough to keep the paper in the promising-not-settled bucket.

The third paper is Model-based analysis of stop-signal data reveals robust neural and clinical correlates of evidence accumulation but not inhibition. This is not a neuromodulation trial, but it is exactly the kind of computational psychiatry paper that helps clean up intervention logic. Using a more mechanistic stop-signal model in the large IMAGEN cohort, the authors argue that substance-use vulnerability tracks evidence accumulation efficiency and related network features better than conventional inhibition metrics. The paper is mostly an engineering platform study, but it addresses a real bottleneck for wearable transcranial ultrasound: conformal fit plus dynamic focusing on irregular surfaces. It matters less as proof of neuromodulation efficacy than as a constraint-solving device paper that could make future adaptive ultrasound work less fake.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that target names are cheap, but state variables, evoked responses, and physically credible interfaces are harder and more valuable. The temporal interference depression paper matters because it at least tries to explain heterogeneity instead of treating deep targeting as self-justifying. The iTBS paper matters because it measures the brain’s response to stimulation rather than only cataloging baseline correlates. The stop-signal modeling paper matters because it suggests many psychiatric intervention stories may be aimed at the wrong latent construct. And the ultrasound hardware paper matters because adaptive neuromodulation remains partly a device-credibility problem, not just a modeling problem.

The most relevant paper today is Closed-Loop Vagus Nerve Stimulation Delivered With a Miniaturized System Produces Lasting Recovery in Individuals With Chronic Stroke. This is one of the more credible translational uses of closed-loop vagus nerve stimulation because the therapy is yoked to rehabilitation events rather than sold as vague autonomic wellness tech. Nineteen chronic ischemic-stroke participants were implanted in a randomized sham-controlled study. The device is much smaller than legacy systems, supports sensor-based triggering, and in the trial it showed a tolerable safety profile with about a five-point upper-extremity Fugl-Meyer gain after active therapy. That is promising, but it is still a small study with investigator conflicts and a combined device-plus-rehabilitation package rather than a clean biomarker-guided controller.

The second paper is Multiscale Mechanisms of Human Memory Modulation by Deep Brain Stimulation. This preprint is mechanistically interesting because it does not treat hippocampal DBS as one knob. Instead it claims that fifty-hertz stimulation in hippocampal white matter improved spatial-sequence memory, while five-hertz stimulation in hippocampal gray matter impaired it, and that both effects can be described through two linked mechanisms: region-specific theta modulation that depends on engagement state, plus global shifts in cortical memory-representation fidelity. It is still early and abstract-level, but the state-dependent and pathway-dependent framing is exactly the kind of intervention logic worth preserving.

The third paper is Brain stimulation prevents neural downregulation and optimizes learning. This is a healthy-cohort transcranial random-noise stimulation and functional-MRI study rather than a patient study, so I am keeping it as adjacent inspiration. The useful claim is that parietal stimulation may work by preventing an early training-related drop in activity within the dorsal-ventral attention network under high attentional load. That is a more specific and more falsifiable framing than generic statements that stimulation simply boosts plasticity.

A fourth item, Personalizing Brain Stimulation for Psychiatric Disorders: From Circuits to Closed-Loop Control, stayed below note threshold. It is a decent review-level citation for where the field wants to go, but it does not add enough new mechanism to earn a preserved note today.

The stroke VNS trial matters because the stimulation is paired with rehabilitation events in a workable device package. The memory DBS preprint matters because it treats stimulation effects as pathway-specific and state-dependent rather than monolithic. The tRNS learning paper is less clinically direct, but it offers a practical hypothesis for why some noninvasive protocols help only under the right task regime: they may preserve usable network excitability when training would otherwise downregulate it too early.

The most relevant paper today is Experimental Validation of Finite Element Models for Directional DBS: The Critical Role of Boundary Conditions on VTA Accuracy. A lot of DBS planning and interpretation work quietly treats field models as if the implementation details are interchangeable. This paper says they are not. In a saline-phantom validation of a directional Boston Scientific lead, the best-matching finite-element setup used a voltage boundary condition with a grounded implantable pulse-generator surface, while conventional current-density formulations substantially overestimated spread. The important point is not just that one simulation stack wins. It is that widely used assumptions can distort the geometry clinicians and researchers think they are stimulating.

The second paper is An Implantable Wireless Battery-Free Selective Vagus Nerve Stimulator. This is still early and mostly a platform paper, but it addresses a real bottleneck in vagus nerve stimulation: therapeutic dosing is often limited by off-target activation. The device is an NFC-controlled, wirelessly powered, temporary multichannel implant built from off-the-shelf parts. In pigs it produced selective bradycardia, and in a single human pilot the authors report separation of cardiac efferent, cardiac afferent, and laryngeal effects. That is not proof of clinical benefit, but it is the kind of interface-level selectivity that matters more than generic "bioelectronic medicine" rhetoric.

The third paper is Developmental and aging changes in brain network switching dynamics revealed by EEG phase synchronization. This is not directly a neuromodulation paper, so I am keeping it as adjacent inspiration rather than a preserved intervention note. Its value is that it ties lifespan differences in phase-synchrony switching to a structural-connectome-constrained oscillator model with an intermediate metastable regime in young adults. That framing is useful for intervention logic because it treats brain-state flexibility as a dynamical-regime problem rather than just another descriptive connectivity statistic.

A fourth paper stayed below full-note threshold but is worth remembering: Rapid rescue of despair behaviors by sonogenetic neuromodulation of the mPFC-DRN pathway. The circuit logic is clean in mice, but because it depends on engineered mechanosensitive channel expression, it is much more a circuit-probe result than an immediately useful therapeutic roadmap.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that intervention logic gets stronger when the physical and dynamical assumptions are made explicit. The DBS finite-element paper matters because it validates the simulation layer that many targeting claims rest on. The selective VNS paper matters because it tries to separate fibers and functions rather than merely stimulating the whole nerve harder. The EEG switching paper is adjacent rather than direct, but it offers a better language for state flexibility and regime selection than the usual static-network summaries.

The most relevant paper today is Multimodal Image Guidance in Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease. A lot of imaging-guided DBS work is decorative because it predicts between-patient outcomes while clinicians still have to test contacts manually. This paper at least aims at the harder, more clinically meaningful problem: discriminating among candidate contacts within patients. Using coordinates, electric fields, tract activations, and structural plus functional network features inside a combined ridge-regression framework, the authors report modest group-level variance explained in unseen data but substantially better contact-ranking performance at the individual level, identifying the optimal contact or a neighboring contact in all but one case. That is not magical precision programming, but it is enough to matter.

The second paper is Non-invasive Neuromodulation Targeting Approach by Mapping Stimulations and Lesions That Modify Visual Memory. This is not a trial, but it is a good example of network-guided target discovery that does more than gesture vaguely at "memory circuits." Across TMS, penetrating head trauma, ischemic stroke, and an independent Alzheimer's-related replication dataset, the authors claim that lesions and stimulation sites associated with visual-memory change converge onto a specific network, with effect direction flipping by age at stimulation or injury. The attractive part is not that it nominates one perfect site. It is that it uses convergent perturbation logic and then translates that into candidate TMS target maps.

The third paper is Transcranial temporal interference stimulation targeting the subthalamic region for motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease: a pilot, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover study. This is exactly the kind of result that invites overclaiming, so restraint matters. The good news is that a single individualized twenty-minute session in thirty medication-off patients beat sham on short-term MDS-UPDRS-III change and responder rate without obvious safety problems. The bad news is that it is still one small acute-effect study, and temporal-interference targeting claims remain anatomically and mechanistically contentious.

A fourth paper stayed below full-note threshold but was worth scanning: Higher-order intrinsic routes support flexible task-evoked communication. It is a strong network-neuroscience idea — task-specific communication as selective recruitment of higher-order resting-state routes rather than wholesale rewiring — but it is still some distance from direct intervention logic, so I kept it as adjacent inspiration instead of a preserved note.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern today is that targeting papers are worthwhile only when they help an actual intervention decision. The image-guided STN DBS paper clears that bar because it tries to rank contacts within patients and gets plausible if still modest results. The visual-memory mapping paper matters because it uses perturbation convergence across lesions and stimulation to derive candidate noninvasive targets, with an important age interaction rather than a fake universal map. The temporal-interference Parkinson's study is promising but still pilot-scale; it should update curiosity, not confidence.

digests.theme: Today is a communication-architecture, pathological-dynamics, and modest-human-evidence day. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is A walk-sum framework of frequency-dependent brain communication architecture. This is a network-computational paper rather than a stimulation trial, but it earns top rank because it gives a sharper intervention backdrop than most applied neuromodulation papers. The core claim is that the structural connectome itself induces a frequency-dependent transfer function, and that this topology-derived resolvent predicts how communication channels distribute across space and frequency without needing a pile of fitted dynamical machinery. The authors report a near-12.6-hertz crossover, strong agreement with MEG eigenmodes across three datasets totaling 912 people, supporting evidence from intracranial EEG in 90 epilepsy patients, alpha-channel collapse under propofol, and altered scaffold exposure in schizophrenia. If that holds up, it matters because intervention logic should care not only about which nodes are connected, but about which frequencies recruit which communication channels through the graph.

The second paper is Deep brain stimulation reduces subthalamic nucleus pathological dynamics and rescues gait deficits associated with dopamine loss. This is mouse work, so it is not a clinical efficacy paper, but it is the kind of mechanistic preclinical DBS study worth preserving. Simultaneous subthalamic recordings and intermittent DBS during locomotion suggest that dopamine loss exaggerates movement encoding, elevates resting beta-rhythmic firing, and creates pathological population dynamics that DBS then suppresses. The strong part is not just that gait improves. It is that therapeutic benefit is linked to reduction of beta-rhythmic spiking and desynchronization of the subthalamic network.

The third paper is A functional MRI and magnetoencephalography study of the cognitive modulatory effect of transcranial direct current stimulation in early Alzheimer's disease. This is the most clinical paper today, but it is also the softest. Forty patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer's disease received anodal left dorsolateral prefrontal stimulation, with pre-post resting-state fMRI, task fMRI, and MEG analyses. The paper reports reduced left middle frontal to posterior cingulate and precuneus resting connectivity, increased posterior cingulate and right middle frontal task activation during memory operations, reduced occipital gamma power, and increased entorhinal theta-gamma coupling after stimulation. That is mechanistically interesting, but without a stronger control design it is hard to know how much of the cognitive modulation story is specific to stimulation rather than time, task familiarity, or generic pre-post drift.

A fourth paper stayed below full-note threshold but was worth scanning: Rapid rescue of despair behaviors by sonogenetic neuromodulation of the mPFC-DRN pathway. The circuit logic is neat, but the translational value is still constrained by the genetic-engineering dependency and by the familiar gap between mouse despair assays and durable depression treatment.
digests.takeaway: The useful theme today is that good neuromodulation papers either clarify the communication scaffold or identify a concrete pathological dynamic they can move. The walk-sum paper is the strongest because it says frequency-specific communication architecture may be analytically constrained by connectome topology, which is the kind of claim that can actually inform intervention reasoning. The subthalamic DBS paper matters because it ties gait rescue to beta-rhythmic spiking reduction and network desynchronization instead of to hand-wavy activation talk. The Alzheimer's tDCS paper is worth keeping, but mainly as a reminder that multimodal correlates are not the same thing as strong causal intervention evidence.

digests.theme: Today is a direct-subcortical targeting, network-embedding, and state-transition logic day. digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound amygdala neuromodulation: a double-blind sham-controlled target engagement study and unblinded single-arm clinical trial. The paper is not a definitive efficacy trial, and it should not be pitched that way. What makes it worth preserving is that it actually earns the translational framing. In the target-engagement phase, MRI-guided focused ultrasound to the left amygdala reduced amygdala BOLD signal relative to sham in a double-blind within-subject design and produced patient-specific hippocampal and insular effects. In the open-label treatment phase, the same patient cohort underwent fifteen sessions over three weeks, tolerated the intervention without serious adverse events, and showed meaningful symptom reductions plus reduced amygdala reactivity to emotional faces. The open-label treatment piece is vulnerable to expectancy and regression-to-the-mean, but the deep-target engagement evidence is much stronger than the average noninvasive-psychiatry paper.

The second paper is Structural and Functional Connectivity Predict the Effects of Direct Brain Stimulation on Memory. This is a good example of a genuinely useful network paper because it does not stop at saying that timing matters. The authors analyze fifty epilepsy patients across sixty-one intracranial stimulation sessions and show that closed-loop stimulation delivered during classifier-detected poor encoding states improves recall on average, but only reliably when the stimulated left temporal site is structurally embedded in a distributed verbal-encoding network. Functional connectivity trends in the same direction, but structural embedding carries the stronger signal. That is exactly the kind of result that sharpens intervention logic: adaptive control without the right circuit scaffold is not enough.

The third paper is Beyond where: When and how brain stimulation drives state transitions. This is a mechanistic modeling preprint rather than an intervention paper, but it earns attention because the question is right. Using subject-specific whole-brain Hopf models fit to MEG across frequency bands, the authors ask why some regions are more responsive to stimulation, when they are most responsive, and whether the best targets for moving between brain states are defined by function labels or by dynamics. Their answer is the more interesting one: optimal nodes depend on dynamical regime, with responsiveness shaped by oscillation radius, temporal variability, state, and frequency band. That does not immediately hand you a clinic-ready protocol, but it is a better control-theoretic frame than the usual static target folklore.

A fourth paper stayed below new-note threshold but still matters as adjacent methods framing: Multimodal Imaging-Based Targeting Approach for Network-Level Brain Stimulation. It offers a sensible fMRI-based workflow for deciding whether a nominal focal tDCS target actually overlaps task-relevant network territory, but right now it reads more like a useful targeting scaffold than a decisive intervention result.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all reject one-dimensional targeting logic. The amygdala focused-ultrasound study matters because it shows that noninvasive deep-target psychiatry becomes more believable when target engagement is measured directly and repeated dosing is at least feasible. The memory-stimulation paper matters because it shows that adaptive timing is not magic if the electrode sits outside the relevant network scaffold. The state-transition modeling paper matters because it says optimal targets may be defined less by named brain regions than by subject-specific dynamical regime. Taken together, the useful lesson is that precision neuromodulation needs three things at once: a reachable target, the right network embedding, and the right state logic.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-16
digests.theme: Today is a pathways, perturbation-readouts, and causal subcortical access day. The strongest translational paper is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression, because it tries to explain depression-TMS efficacy in terms of multi-step structural routes rather than treating anti-subgenual connectivity as a magical scalar. The strongest computational-clinical paper is A deep representation learning model to predict response to vagus nerve stimulation, because it moves beyond weak presurgical clinical predictors and uses routine structural MRI to learn a response model with at least some biological interpretability. The strongest methods-mechanism paper is Low-intensity focused ultrasound to human amygdala reveals a causal role in ambiguous emotion processing and alters local and network activity, because it actually perturbs a deep affective structure in humans and couples the behavioral claim to target-engagement readouts.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression. The abstract is compact, but the claim is important. Rather than asking only whether a dorsolateral prefrontal cortex site is anticorrelated with subgenual cingulate in resting fMRI, the authors use connectome modeling to propose polysynaptic cortical and subcortical routes linking stimulation sites to subgenual cingulate through intermediate nodes. Their main result is that route length explains treatment response in two independent patient cohorts and also tracks the efficacy of functional-MRI-guided targeting. The useful read is not that the field has solved precision TMS. It is that stimulation efficacy may depend on traversable anatomical communication paths, not just on one resting-connectivity number. That matters because it pushes targeting logic toward mechanism and away from sloganized anti-subgenual heuristics.

The second paper is A deep representation learning model to predict response to vagus nerve stimulation. This is clinically useful because it starts from an honest baseline: in the largest reported pediatric VNS cohort, presurgical clinical variables alone did not predict response better than chance. The authors then use routine preoperative T1-weighted MRI from a substantial imaging cohort, pretrain on thousands of structural scans to learn compact anatomic representations, and report an AUC of 0.73 for VNS response prediction. The interpretability story is not fully causal, but it is better than average. Model saliency reportedly localizes to serotonin-rich regions, and nonresponders show inferred large-scale network disruption. This is exactly the kind of paper that matters for intervention logic: not because it is clinically solved, but because it pairs practical input data with a predictor that at least gestures toward identifiable circuitry.

The third paper is Low-intensity focused ultrasound to human amygdala reveals a causal role in ambiguous emotion processing and alters local and network activity. This is not a psychiatric trial, and it would be silly to sell it as one. What it does do is more valuable at this stage: it shows that low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound can perturb the human basolateral amygdala, change resting-state connectivity and local spectroscopy-derived excitation-inhibition balance, and shift behavior on an emotional-learning task in a stimulation-volume-dependent way. The key behavioral result is increased approach toward neutral, emotionally ambiguous faces plus slowed responses to neutral and happy faces after basolateral amygdala stimulation. That is a real mechanistic advance because it moves deep noninvasive neuromodulation from vague possibility toward specific causal perturbation with convergent readouts.

A fourth paper stayed below new-note threshold but still matters as context: Association of Brain Network Perturbations With Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Children With Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy. It is already in the repo, and it still helps frame today’s VNS predictor paper because it argues that response heterogeneity lives partly in network resilience, not just in clinical labels.
digests.takeaway: The best work today converges on a simple lesson: neuromodulation claims become more credible when the paper says how the effect could travel, what latent state or circuit feature it is actually reading, and whether the perturbation reaches the intended deep system at all. The TMS pathways paper matters because it makes structural communication routes part of the targeting story. The VNS predictor paper matters because it starts from the failure of easy clinical baselines and then uses routine MRI to build a more informative response model. The amygdala ultrasound paper matters because it supplies rare human causal evidence at a deep affective target with more than one readout. Overall, this is a good day for mechanism over folklore.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-15
digests.theme: Today is a stop treating targeting folklore as validation day. The strongest clinical-translational keep is Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study, because it is a useful corrective to the field’s habit of treating anti-subgenual targeting as if it were already settled truth. The strongest methods paper is Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI, because it tries to replace correlational target rhetoric with empirically evoked circuit maps. The strongest computational-network paper is Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals, which matters because most control models still pretend stimulation acts on isolated nodes even though real stimulation spreads in space.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study. This is a prospective multisite observational test of one of the most repeated ideas in depression TMS: that left-DLPFC sites with stronger negative functional connectivity to subgenual cingulate should produce better antidepressant outcomes. Sixty-six patients with major depressive disorder received three to eight weeks of routine clinical left-DLPFC rTMS, with actual stimulation sites recorded by MRI neuronavigation. The cleanest result is negative. Normative subgenual-connectivity of the delivered site did not predict symptom improvement on its own, and most explained variance came instead from baseline anxiety and psychiatric comorbidity. That does not mean network targeting is useless. It does mean the simple anti-subgenual heuristic looks too thin for real-world heterogeneous clinics.

The second paper is Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI. Over more than eighty participants, the authors used personalized cortical targets intended to engage either subgenual anterior cingulate cortex or basolateral amygdala, then measured TMS-evoked BOLD responses while controlling for motion, pain, and somatosensory confounds. The useful result is not that they discovered a magic psychiatric target. It is that image-guided TMS can produce reproducible distributed downstream responses and that the resulting maps can serve as a more causal complement to resting-connectivity target stories.

The third paper is Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals. This is not a stimulation trial, but it is exactly the kind of network-control paper that improves intervention logic. The authors modify optimal-control models so inputs spread spatially with exponential distance decay instead of acting only on single nodes. Under that more realistic assumption, state transitions often require much less energy and many fewer effective input signals, and the derived input-density maps align with independent functional, metabolic, genetic, and neurochemical annotations. The paper matters because real brain stimulation is spatially blurry, and control theory that ignores that blur may be optimizing the wrong object.

A fourth paper stayed below note threshold but remains useful citation material: Clinical utility and prospective of TMS-EEG: Updated review from an international expert group. It is broad and competent, but it is still a review rather than a preserve-worthy mechanistic advance.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all punish overconfident targeting narratives. The depression-TMS cohort study says a famous normative-connectivity heuristic is much less robust in real clinics than people often imply. The interleaved TMS/fMRI paper says if you want to talk about circuits, you should measure stimulation-evoked circuit consequences rather than stopping at resting correlations. And the spatially diffuse control paper says control theory should stop pretending that stimulation enters the brain as perfectly local node-wise impulses. Overall lesson: better intervention logic will require more causal measurement, more realistic control assumptions, and more respect for clinical heterogeneity.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-14
digests.theme: Today is a network-level reconfiguration, not target folklore day. The strongest keep is Frequency-Dependent Whole-Brain Reconfiguration Following Left DLPFC rTMS in Older Adults: A 106-Channel fNIRS Study, because it does something a lot of noninvasive stimulation papers still avoid: it measures distributed network consequences of the same nominal target under different frequencies instead of pretending “1 Hz inhibits, 10 Hz excites” is already a mechanistic explanation. The strongest methods paper is cuBNM: GPU-Accelerated Brain Network Modeling, because it attacks a real bottleneck in individualized whole-brain modeling rather than selling one more decorative AI wrapper. The most interesting adjacent theory paper is Structured flexibility in recurrent neural networks via neuromodulation, which is not an intervention paper, but it is useful for thinking about how low-dimensional modulatory signals can gate network computation without needing full weight rewrites.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Frequency-Dependent Whole-Brain Reconfiguration Following Left DLPFC rTMS in Older Adults: A 106-Channel fNIRS Study. Thirty healthy older adults underwent both 10 hertz and 1 hertz left-dorsolateral-prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in a randomized single-blind crossover design, with whole-brain resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy before and immediately after stimulation. The clean result is not that one frequency was simply excitatory and the other inhibitory. At the network-summary level, 10 hertz tended toward more globally positive topology and distributed-connectivity changes, while 1 hertz tended the other way, but localized paradoxical effects also appeared, including bilateral primary-motor-cortex increases after 1 hertz and decreases after 10 hertz. That makes this paper useful less as a clinical efficacy claim and more as a reminder that stimulation effects are distributed, state-dependent, and not well described by a crude frequency slogan.

The second paper is cuBNM: GPU-Accelerated Brain Network Modeling. This is a methods infrastructure paper, but a respectable one. The authors build a GPU-based Python package for large-scale brain network model simulation and fitting, then show several-hundred-fold speedups over CPU baselines while supporting group-level and individualized optimization in low- and high-dimensional models. The useful read is not “faster is always better.” The useful read is that individualized network-model fitting may be becoming cheap enough to test as part of targeting, subject stratification, or intervention-design workflows instead of living mostly as boutique offline analysis.

The third paper is Structured flexibility in recurrent neural networks via neuromodulation. This is adjacent inspiration rather than a direct neuromodulation paper. In a low-rank recurrent-neural-network setup, a neuromodulatory subnetwork emits low-dimensional gain signals that dynamically scale recurrent weights, improving training and generalization on canonical tasks and yielding gating behavior that the authors relate to standard artificial recurrent-network mechanisms. The reason to keep it in view is not biological realism theater. It is that the paper offers a compact computational picture of how low-dimensional modulatory control could reorganize network computation without full structural rewiring.

One paper stayed below note threshold today despite being visible in scouting: Proceedings of the 12th annual deep brain stimulation think tank: cutting edge technology meets novel applications. It is useful citation material if you want a broad snapshot of where the DBS establishment thinks the field is headed, but it is still a proceedings overview, not a paper I would preserve as a primary mechanistic note.
digests.takeaway: The most useful papers today all punish oversimplification. The rTMS study matters because distributed network effects in aging brains do not collapse neatly into a single excitatory-versus-inhibitory rule. cuBNM matters because personalized network modeling only becomes consequential when it is cheap enough to run at real scale. The low-rank neuromodulated-RNN paper matters because it offers a compact computational story for how small modulatory control signals can reshape network behavior. Overall lesson: if the field wants better intervention logic, it needs both better whole-brain measurement and cheaper mechanistic modeling, not just louder target branding.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-13
digests.theme: Today is a mechanism-over-magic neuromodulation day. The strongest translational paper is mPFC axons drive cognitive control enhancement during striatal stimulation, because it stops treating ventral-capsule or ventral-striatal stimulation as a black-box psychiatric target and asks which circuit element is actually carrying the cognitive benefit. The strongest clinical paper is Treatment of Persisting Symptoms after Concussion with Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Double-Blinded, Randomized, Controlled Trial, not because it is positive, but because it is a useful clean negative: twenty sessions of left-dorsolateral-prefrontal high-frequency rTMS did not beat sham on the main symptom endpoint. The strongest control-methods paper is Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG, because it addresses a real bottleneck in online stimulation: most phase-targeting systems assume periodic rhythms and struggle with brief task-locked activity. The strongest network psychiatry paper is Brain Functional Connectivity Signatures of Craving Across Substance Use Disorders: A Transdiagnostic Approach, because it at least tries to move craving from diagnosis-specific storytelling toward a distributed predictive network that generalizes across cohorts.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is mPFC axons drive cognitive control enhancement during striatal stimulation. This is the one to keep because it sharpens intervention logic instead of just reporting that stimulation helped behavior. In a rodent set-shift task, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation of medial-prefrontal axons in the striatum reproduced the faster response times previously seen with electrical stimulation, while direct stimulation of local striatal neurons impaired performance with sustained use. The paper then links within-session decline in benefit to reduced evoked responses and weaker post-stimulation circuit responsiveness. The useful claim is that at least part of the cognitive-control effect of ventral-striatal-like stimulation is being driven by recruited cortical afferents rather than local striatal cell bodies. That matters for targeting, waveform design, and how not to lie to ourselves about mechanism.

The second paper is Treatment of Persisting Symptoms after Concussion with Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Double-Blinded, Randomized, Controlled Trial. This is a proper reminder that clinical neuromodulation needs more than plausible targets and patient suffering. Ninety-one adults with persistent post-concussion symptoms were randomized to active or sham left-dorsolateral-prefrontal rTMS across twenty sessions. Both groups improved over time, but active stimulation did not significantly outperform sham on the Rivermead Postconcussion Symptoms Questionnaire at post-treatment, one month, or three months. The useful read is not that rTMS never matters here. It is that this specific open-loop recipe did not separate from expectancy and nonspecific care effects, which should lower confidence in generic DLPFC carryover from depression logic.

The third paper is Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG. This is a methods preprint, but it hits the right problem. Instead of predicting oscillatory phase from highly periodic signals, the authors directly detect phase in real time and report microsecond-scale triggering. In simulations and human EEG without active TMS delivery, the system achieved higher triggering probability and lower phase-error variability than a prediction-based baseline, especially for event-related theta during spatial-navigation tasks. The meaningful claim is that precision phase-locked stimulation may be able to leave the comfort zone of ongoing alpha rhythms and target briefer cognitive states.

The fourth paper is Brain Functional Connectivity Signatures of Craving Across Substance Use Disorders: A Transdiagnostic Approach. In resting-state functional MRI from people with cannabis, opioid, and tobacco use disorders, the authors use connectome-based predictive modeling to derive a distributed craving network that predicts self-reported craving and then generalizes to external alcohol-dependence and smoker datasets. The useful part is the transdiagnostic ambition and the lesion analysis highlighting medial orbitofrontal, dorsal posterior cingulate, and medial frontal contributions. The caution is that this is still a resting-state predictive signature, not a causal circuit map or a clinically deployed relapse model.

Two additional papers were worth reading but stayed below note threshold today. Experimental Validation of Finite Element Models for Directional DBS: The Critical Role of Boundary Conditions on VTA Accuracy is useful citation material because it shows that common current-controlled modeling assumptions can badly overestimate activated volume. Multiscale reorganization of brain and behavior under large-scale electrical perturbation is ambitious and potentially framing-relevant, but right now it reads more like a large synthesis-and-association map than something I would center a daily intervention digest around.
digests.takeaway: The better papers today are the ones that cash out mechanism into something testable. The striatal-stimulation paper matters because it separates recruited cortical afferents from local neurons and shows that those are not interchangeable. The concussion trial matters because it refuses the usual neuromodulation optimism and shows a clinically plausible recipe can still fail against sham. The closed-loop TMS-EEG paper matters because timing precision for brief event-related states is a real control problem, not a side detail. The craving-network paper matters because transdiagnostic predictive structure is more useful than diagnosis-by-diagnosis craving folklore, even if it is still not causal. Overall lesson: intervention logic gets sharper when we ask what element, what state, and what benchmark actually changed.
