The authors assembled a retrospective multicenter cohort of 115 patients across 12 centers, spanning thalamic, pallidal, and subthalamic DBS, localized electrodes with an imaging pipeline, and applied voxel-wise sweetspot mapping to identify regions associated with tic improvement. Because the resulting response maps visually followed fiber trajectories, they then interpreted them anatomically against specific pallidothalamic and thalamostriatal bundles. Their main claim is that tic-response peaks across the three targets align with a common structural pathway logic, and that this cross-target mapping explains outcomes better than treating each target as an isolated therapy.
notes.whyItMatters: Because this is the kind of paper that makes neuromodulation targeting more legible. It does not solve Tourette DBS, but it pushes the field toward a transferable circuit logic: different targets may be useful because they touch overlapping therapeutic fibers, not because each nucleus has its own isolated magic.
notes.finalDecision: Keep this as a strong targeting reference and a good example of cross-target mechanistic framing. Useful now for thinking, and potentially more useful later if prospective validation appears.

notes.title: Efficacy of Personalized Connectivity-Guided Accelerated Brain Stimulation in a Naturalistic Treatment-Resistant Depression Population
notes.whySelected: It is a current example of personalized accelerated TMS being pushed into a more comorbid real-world depression population, but with much weaker evidence than the precision-psychiatry framing implies.
notes.verdictText: This is worth preserving as a translational signal, not as proof. The targeting rationale is sensible enough — choose near-scalp targets within attentional networks that maximize anti-correlation with sgACC and then run an accelerated iTBS schedule — but the study is small, uncontrolled, and leans heavily on historical comparison plus post-hoc electric-field modeling. The right read is “interesting and hypothesis-generating,” not “personalized TMS is now solved.”
notes.overview: The paper asks whether a SAINT-like personalized accelerated iTBS strategy can retain efficacy when moved from tightly curated Western research cohorts into a naturalistic Asian treatment-resistant depression population with heavy psychiatric comorbidity. Twenty participants received 50 sessions over five days using a method the authors call TAO-TMS, which selects individualized cortical targets intended to maximize anti-correlation with subgenual anterior cingulate cortex while also preferring near-scalp sites that reduce required stimulation intensity. They report a 70% response rate overall, 83% in a cleaner trial-eligible subgroup, heterogeneous participant-level connectivity changes, and a post-hoc electric-field modeling claim that the personalized targets improved network focality relative to BeamF3. That is enough to keep the paper, but not enough to treat it as decisive efficacy evidence.
notes.whyItMatters: Because precision-neuromodulation claims often get louder as designs get weaker. This paper is useful exactly because it sits at that tension point: some of the intervention logic is sensible, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to justify the packaging. Keeping notes like this helps separate real targeting ideas from branding inflation.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful but weak paper. Good for framing and for watching the personalized accelerated TMS literature, but not for strong efficacy claims.

notes.title: Towards connectome-guided optimization of deep brain stimulation for gait dysfunction
notes.whySelected: It turns a common DBS complaint — good control of other Parkinsonian symptoms but poor gait response — into an explicit contact-and-parameter optimization problem tied to a symptom-specific connectome.
notes.verdictText: This is the strongest intervention-logic paper in today’s batch. It is not definitive clinical evidence, because most of the support comes from retrospective alignment between algorithmic recommendations and previously chosen clinical settings, plus a tiny six-patient reprogramming illustration. But unlike vague “AI optimization” packaging, this paper specifies what is being optimized, why gait may need different contacts than other symptoms, and how a symptom-specific network could alter programming.
notes.overview: The paper addresses a practical failure mode of Parkinson’s DBS: contacts and settings that help tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia do not necessarily help gait dysfunction. The authors build an algorithm that takes electrode location and modeled stimulation volume, then chooses contacts and parameters to maximize overlap with circuitry previously associated with gait improvement. They train and test this idea in two independent STN-DBS cohorts whose settings had already been clinically optimized, then compare the algorithm’s preferred gait-oriented stimulation volumes with the settings clinicians actually chose. The striking result is that the gait-optimized volumes differ substantially from real-world programming in most patients, yet the degree of similarity between the algorithmic and clinical volumes correlates with gait benefit, and a tiny proof-of-concept reprogramming set suggests the recommendations may be usable.
notes.whyItMatters: Because this is exactly the kind of paper that makes closed-loop or adaptive neuromodulation feel less like branding and more like engineering. It isolates a symptom, proposes an objective function, and tests whether clinical settings are even solving the right problem.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is a good example of connectome-guided programming with real translational value, even though the prospective clinical evidence is still early.

notes.title: A multicenter randomized clinical trial of portable transcranial alternating current stimulation for major depressive disorder
notes.whySelected: It is a sham-controlled multicenter depression trial for portable bilateral DLPFC HD-tACS, which makes it more decision-relevant than the usual tiny feasibility stimulation paper.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more practically consequential neuromodulation papers surfaced today because it is not just another open-label stimulation report. A 120-person randomized sham-controlled multicenter trial for portable HD-tACS in major depression is enough to pay attention to. The caveat is that the paper still looks much stronger on efficacy signal than on mechanism: the abstract supports a clinical effect, but it does not yet explain why 10 Hz bilateral DLPFC stimulation should be the right control variable, and the two hypomania cases matter.
notes.overview: The trial tests whether a portable, low-intensity 10 Hz high-definition transcranial alternating current stimulation protocol aimed at bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can improve depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder. One hundred twenty participants were randomized 1:1 to active or sham stimulation and completed 20 sessions over four weeks, followed by four weeks of additional follow-up. The active arm showed a larger reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores than sham, with the abstract also reporting benefits in anxiety, sleep efficiency, and several quality-of-life domains. That makes this more than a decorative device paper, but the accessible text is mostly outcome-focused, so confidence is much lower on target-engagement logic, blinding robustness, and whether the chosen frequency and montage are mechanistically justified rather than empirically selected.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the sort of paper that can distort discourse if read lazily. The clinical signal looks more serious than most tACS depression papers, but the mechanism is still under-articulated. It is worth keeping both for translational opportunity and as a reminder that outcome signal without targeting logic is only half the story.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is one of the more decision-relevant noninvasive depression stimulation papers surfaced recently, but it still needs a fuller read before treating it as strong mechanistic evidence or a settled clinical protocol.

notes.title: Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided randomized trial
notes.whySelected: It is a useful negative trial showing that a plausible connectivity-guided targeting heuristic did not outperform standard M1 rTMS, while still hinting that a narrower local connectivity biomarker may matter.
notes.verdictText: This is not a win for personalization, and that is exactly why it is worth keeping. The authors ran a randomized, double-blind chronic pain trial and found that their global connectivity-guided target selection strategy did not improve outcomes over classic M1 stimulation. The interesting residue is that lower local M1 connectivity predicted better response within the standard M1 arm, which suggests the biomarker may have been too coarse or aimed at the wrong physiological level.
notes.overview: This paper asks whether rTMS target selection for chronic pain can be improved by measuring cortical connectivity before therapy and then assigning patients to a stimulation site based on that physiology instead of just using the classic primary motor cortex target. The connectivity measure came from TMS-evoked EEG phase-locking across four candidate targets: primary motor cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and posterosuperior insula. Ninety patients with chronic pain were randomized to a low-connectivity targeting arm, a high-connectivity targeting arm, or a classic-M1 arm, and they received 12 sessions over 8 weeks. The main result is negative: the connectivity-guided allocation rule did not improve the primary endpoint or the secondary outcomes relative to standard M1 stimulation. But exploratory analyses suggest that lower local baseline connectivity within M1 may predict greater pain reduction in the classic-M1 group, which leaves behind a potentially more specific biomarker story even though the headline personalization strategy failed.
notes.whyItMatters: Because negative personalization trials are a gift. They tell us where a plausible intervention logic breaks, and they help prevent biomarker theater from being mistaken for actual treatment improvement. For us, that is valuable because failed targeting heuristics are often more instructive than glossy retrospective success stories.
notes.finalDecision: Keep this as a useful corrective paper. The main targeting idea failed, but the failure is informative, and the local-connectivity signal is worth tracking without turning it into a triumph.

notes.title: Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans
notes.whySelected: It is one of the clearest recent attempts to map DBS effects at the individual circuit level across frequencies and timescales rather than treating neuromodulation as a black box with symptom readouts.
notes.verdictText: This is a real mechanism paper, not just a clinical outcome paper wearing a circuit costume. The authors collect unusually rich longitudinal imaging from individual Parkinson patients with MRI-compatible STN-DBS and use that density to estimate personalized networks, stimulation responses, and target-cortical connectivity. The sample is still modest and the work is Parkinson’s-specific, but the study meaningfully advances how one should study neuromodulation mechanisms in humans.
notes.overview: The paper asks what circuits STN deep brain stimulation actually modulates in individual Parkinson’s disease patients, and whether those circuit responses vary by stimulation frequency and over the course of treatment. To answer that, the authors use a 3-T MRI-compatible DBS system and repeatedly scan 14 patients before surgery and then four times over the next year under multiple stimulation conditions, including off stimulation, high-frequency, low-frequency, and variable-frequency DBS. They build individualized cortical parcellations and connectomes, estimate target-cortical functional connectivity from each patient’s stimulation volume, and analyze both resting-state and block-design fMRI responses. The main claim is that DBS engages separable pallidal and motor-cortical circuits with different temporal and frequency signatures, and that individualized target-cortical connectivity carries clinically useful information about motor response.
notes.whyItMatters: Because this is the kind of paper that makes “precision neuromodulation” sound less like branding and more like a measurable engineering problem. It exposes circuit structure, frequency dependence, and person-specific variation in a way that can inform targeting, adaptive control, and translational mechanism work.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a core reference for mechanism-focused neuromodulation work. It does not solve personalization, but it shows what a serious attempt looks like.

notes.title: Deep-learning-assisted simulation of a cortical circuit: integrating anatomy, physiology and function
notes.whySelected: It makes large biologically constrained circuit fitting far more practical, which is exactly what mechanistic computational neuroscience keeps claiming to want.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the better recent computational neuroscience papers because the deep-learning part is in service of a real bottleneck rather than branding. The contribution is not a new decoder benchmark; it is a differentiable simulator plus a large multimodal V1 model that can actually be optimized under biological constraints on commodity hardware. That does not solve identifiability or make mouse V1 automatically translational, but it materially improves the feasibility of mechanism-oriented circuit modeling.
notes.overview: The paper builds a roughly 67,000-neuron recurrent spiking model of mouse primary visual cortex by integrating EM connectomics, cell-type-resolved electrophysiology, multipatch synaptic physiology, and large-scale Neuropixels recordings. Instead of relying on slow manual tuning, the authors use a GPU-accelerated differentiable simulator and gradient-based optimization to fit the model to in vivo response statistics while preserving biological priors such as synaptic weight distributions and cell-type structure. The trained network reportedly generalizes beyond the narrow training stimuli to new contrasts and natural scenes, and analysis of the fitted parameters highlights structured inhibitory cohorts with outsized control over circuit activity. The main value is not that the model is the final answer; it is that the workflow makes constrained large-scale circuit fitting substantially easier to reproduce, perturb, and criticize.
notes.whyItMatters: Because if we care about mechanism and controllability, we need circuit models that can actually be fit, perturbed, and reused under biological constraints. This is more promising infrastructure than another opaque predictive model.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. Strong computational infrastructure paper with real mechanistic utility, though still more about making serious modeling possible than delivering a direct intervention result.

notes.title: A modular, high-bandwidth, bidirectional implantable device for neural interrogation
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent hardware papers aimed at the actual bottlenecks of chronic bidirectional neuromodulation rather than another narrow single-indication implant story.
notes.verdictText: This is a platform paper, not therapy evidence, so it should be judged as engineering infrastructure rather than clinical impact. On that standard it is solidly useful: the modular fully implantable design, bidirectional communication, and validation with a third-party spinal array all attack real practical barriers to ecological closed-loop neurotechnology. The red flag is the usual one for hardware papers — stable preclinical operation is not the same thing as durable human translational viability.
notes.overview: The authors describe the Modular Bionic Interface (MBI), a fully implantable system paired with a worn external unit that supports wireless power/data transfer, neural recording, and spatiotemporally patterned electrical stimulation through modular connections to third-party implanted devices. The pitch is that most current systems force bad tradeoffs: tethered rigs provide bandwidth but kill ecological use, while fully implanted systems often sacrifice channel count, modularity, or bidirectionality. The MBI is proposed as a compromise architecture that can record high-fidelity electrophysiology and deliver stimulation while remaining implantable and adaptable to different anatomical targets. The paper validates the platform on the benchtop and in a chronic sheep implantation over three months, including evoked motor responses and spinal compound action potential recordings when connected to an actively powered high-resolution spinal cord stimulation array.
notes.whyItMatters: Because serious neuromodulation keeps running into the same boring but decisive infrastructure problem: you need sensing, stimulation, telemetry, and modularity in one system. This paper is useful because it treats that as the main engineering problem instead of pretending clinical magic happens first.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as translational infrastructure. Not a mechanism paper and not efficacy evidence, but the architecture is concrete enough to matter.

notes.title: Prefrontal-bed nucleus of the stria terminalis physiological and neuropsychological biomarkers predict therapeutic outcomes in depression
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent psychiatric DBS papers because it ties depression outcomes to perioperative and longitudinal intracranial biomarkers instead of stopping at target anatomy and response rates.
notes.verdictText: This is not definitive biomarker validation; the cohort is still small and refractory-depression DBS remains a hard place to generalize from. But the paper does a serious version of mechanism-aware clinical neuromodulation: randomized trial structure, invasive signal acquisition, predictive baseline physiology, longitudinal biomarker tracking, and an attempt to connect physiology to tractography and affective phenotype. That puts it above most depression DBS papers, which often gesture at circuits while mostly reporting symptoms.
notes.overview: The authors ran a DBS trial in treatment-refractory depression targeting the BNST/NAc region and asked whether perioperative electrophysiology could predict who benefits. They recorded resting BNST local field potentials and frontal EEG with externalized electrodes, extracted spectral and coupling features, and used correlation analyses plus ridge regression to predict 3-, 6-, and 12-month outcomes. Lower BNST theta power, lower frontal-BNST theta coherence, and stronger top-down prefrontal-to-BNST connectivity predicted better depression and quality-of-life outcomes. In a subset with repeated longitudinal recordings during the blinded crossover period, BNST theta also moved with stimulation state and momentary mood/anxiety, supporting it as more than a one-off baseline correlate.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it upgrades depression DBS from “stimulate an anatomically plausible place and hope” toward a more falsifiable control framework: measure circuit state, predict who benefits, and test whether stimulation changes that state.
notes.finalDecision: Keep and revisit. This is one of the better recent psychiatric DBS papers for people who care about explicit biomarker/control logic, though it is still far from definitive enough to canonize.

notes.title: Precision Network Modeling of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Across Individuals Suggests Therapeutic Targets and Potential for Improvement
notes.whySelected: It is a useful targeting paper because it shows that common TMS placement rules do not reliably engage the same higher-order networks across people and offers an individual-network modeling workflow instead.
notes.verdictText: This is not a clinical efficacy paper, and the title is slightly grander than the evidential reach. But the paper makes a real contribution to intervention logic: it explicitly models which networks standard and individualized dlPFC TMS targets hit in each person, and it shows that common heuristics often miss the intended network or hit mixed network territory. That matters if the field wants to stop pretending “left dlPFC” is a sufficiently precise target description.
notes.overview: The authors combine precision network estimation with transcranial magnetic stimulation electric-field modeling to ask what functional networks are actually stimulated by common clinical dlPFC TMS targets. They compare scalp-landmark targets such as F3/F4, sgACC-anticorrelation targets, and individually optimized coil placements in a dlPFC search space. Across participants, the same nominal target often engages different mixtures of frontoparietal, salience/cingulo-opercular, default, and other association networks. Individual optimization improves spatial selectivity and intensity for the intended network, and the authors argue this can be done from a relatively low-burden single MRI session.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens a core practical question: if you claim network-targeted TMS, can you show which network you are actually hitting in this person? This paper gives a better way to ask and partially answer that question.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as targeting infrastructure and framing. It does not prove therapeutic superiority, but it is useful ammunition against lazy “precision TMS” claims and a plausible template for better targeting workflows.

notes.title: Cell-Type-Specific Bidirectional Modulation of the Cortico-Thalamo-Cortical Sensory Pathway by Transcranial Focused Ultrasound (tFUS)
notes.whySelected: It is a compact recent mechanism paper showing parameter-dependent excitatory versus inhibitory tFUS effects with identified neuronal contributors rather than generic modulation language.
notes.verdictText: This is not a clinical paper and I only inspected the accessible abstract, so confidence should stay bounded. Still, the paper is worth preserving because it makes a much cleaner claim than most ultrasound neuromodulation work: different parameter regimes push the same sensory pathway in opposite directions, and the authors identify a specific cortical excitatory-cell contribution instead of hand-waving about “modulation.”
notes.overview: Using rats, the authors recorded sensory-evoked potentials and multi-unit activity in somatosensory cortex (S1) and posterior medial thalamus during hind-paw tactile stimulation, then applied tFUS to S1 under different ultrasound parameter regimes. Optogenetic tagging identified cortical CaMKII-positive, PV-positive, and SST-positive neurons, while thalamic units were classified as putative excitatory or inhibitory by waveform features. High-PRF/high-duty/high-pressure stimulation produced excitatory modulation of the sensory pathway, whereas lower-PRF/lower-duty/lower-pressure stimulation produced inhibitory modulation. The accessible abstract attributes both directions primarily to changes in S1 CaMKII-positive neuron activity, with corresponding downstream effects in thalamic regular-spiking units.
notes.whyItMatters: Because if ultrasound neuromodulation is going to be more than a bag of inconsistent claims, it needs parameter-to-circuit rules. This paper looks like a modest but real step in that direction.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as adjacent mechanistic reading, with the caveat that this note is abstract-based and should be upgraded only after a fuller read.

notes.title: Long-Term Personalized Adaptive Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson Disease: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
notes.whySelected: It is one of the more important recent clinical steps toward chronic at-home adaptive DBS using implanted sensing rather than short supervised demos.
notes.verdictText: This is not the cleanest causal test of adaptive control logic, but it matters because it shows that long-term aDBS can actually run in the wild, not just in a lab demo. The mechanistic sophistication is modest — mostly thresholded control around α/β-band LFP power — and the primary endpoint required post hoc revision, so this is not a victory lap. Still, as operational evidence that chronic sensing-driven DBS is clinically viable, it is important.
notes.overview: The ADAPT-PD multicenter pivotal trial enrolled Parkinson disease patients already stable on continuous DBS and tested two embedded adaptive DBS modes — single-threshold and dual-threshold control — driven by patient-specific local field potential activity in the α-β range sensed from implanted DBS hardware. Participants underwent setup and adjustment, then evaluation in blinded 30-day mode periods, followed by optional long-term follow-up at home for roughly 10 months. Most participants met the study’s performance goal for maintaining acceptable on-time without troublesome dyskinesia relative to continuous DBS, single-threshold aDBS reduced delivered energy versus cDBS, and serious device-related safety problems were not seen through long-term follow-up.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is evidence that closed-loop DBS can leave the sandbox. Even if the control policy is simple, the study makes adaptive neuromodulation feel more like engineering and less like perpetual prototype theater.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as core reference for practical aDBS translation. Strong on deployment relevance, moderate on mechanistic sharpness, weaker than ideal on confirmatory trial design.

notes.title: Invasive Brain Mapping Identifies Personalized Therapeutic Neuromodulation Targets for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
notes.venue: medRxiv preprint; later updated in Translational Psychiatry
notes.whySelected: It is one of the clearest recent examples of personalized circuit therapeutics where target selection, biomarker logic, and stimulation-induced circuit modulation are all made explicit.
notes.verdictText: This is still a single-patient proof of concept, so no one should confuse it with settled evidence. But the paper does something many neuromodulation studies merely gesture at: it maps candidate sites, identifies a symptom-linked physiological signal, shows that the chosen stimulation sites suppress that signal, and then carries those sites into chronic DBS. If you care about mechanism-aware psychiatric neuromodulation, this is unusually concrete.
notes.overview: The authors implanted temporary stereoelectroencephalography electrodes across cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) regions in a patient with severe treatment-refractory OCD, then used a multi-day inpatient stimulation-mapping protocol to identify sites that acutely improved symptoms. They found two right ventral capsule targets that reduced OCD symptoms during sham-controlled testing. Intracranial recordings suggested that high-frequency activity in orbitofrontal and related CSTC regions tracked symptom severity, and stimulation at the selected ventral capsule sites suppressed orbitofrontal high-frequency activity while showing structural and electrophysiological connectivity to those cortical regions. Those personalized targets were then implanted for chronic DBS, and combined stimulation produced an early clinical improvement.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a serious example of circuit therapeutics instead of decorative personalization rhetoric. It suggests a workflow for psychiatric neuromodulation where target choice is justified by symptom-linked physiology and demonstrated engagement, not just historical habit.
notes.finalDecision: Preserve and revisit. This is one of the better recent exemplars of mechanism-aware psychiatric neuromodulation, but its evidential strength is still proof-of-concept rather than generalizable clinical standard.

notes.title: Closing the loop between brain and electrical stimulation: A proof-of-concept randomized trial of real-time fMRI-guided tACS optimization
notes.whySelected: It is a relatively concrete attempt to personalize noninvasive network stimulation online using neural feedback rather than fixed tACS parameters.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more interesting recent noninvasive closed-loop papers because it actually optimizes stimulation parameters online against a network target. But it is still a small proof-of-concept in healthy participants, the behavioral effect is modest, and the target variable is fMRI functional connectivity during a 2-back task rather than any clinically validated state. Worth watching, not worth worshipping.
notes.overview: The study combines concurrent high-definition dual-site tACS with real-time fMRI and a simplex optimization algorithm to adjust stimulation frequency and phase offset between right DLPFC and right inferior parietal cortex while participants perform a working-memory task. Participants were randomized into an up-regulation arm, where the algorithm searched for stimulation parameters that preserved or increased frontoparietal functional connectivity, and a down-regulation arm, where it searched for parameters that reduced connectivity. After two training runs, the optimized parameter set was applied in a test run. The groups diverged in connectivity trajectories during testing, and the up-regulation group showed better within-run accuracy improvement, with resting-state connectivity changes suggesting some persistence beyond immediate stimulation.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a better prototype of noninvasive precision stimulation than the usual fixed-frequency mush. Even if the setup is cumbersome, the paper makes the intervention logic explicit enough to critique and build on.
notes.finalDecision: Keep, but as an early proof-of-concept rather than a mature translational paper. Good intervention logic, weak sample strength.

notes.title: A Data-Driven Closed-Loop Control Approach to Drive Neural State Transitions for Mechanistic Insight
notes.whySelected: It is a computationally serious attempt to infer controllability of affective-state transitions from learned nonlinear brain dynamics rather than static connectivity alone.
notes.verdictText: This is adjacent rather than directly actionable. The paper is most valuable as a computational framing device for how one might rank targets or estimate control difficulty in psychiatric state transitions. It is not evidence that current neuromodulation systems can reliably steer remitted depression or repetitive negative thinking in the real world.
notes.overview: The authors train subject-level nonlinear dynamical surrogate models on fMRI data recorded during resting and sad mood induction in participants with remitted major depressive disorder and healthy controls. They then define target state distributions using Gaussian mixture models and use model predictive control to infer region-specific control inputs that would drive transitions between affective states in silico. Their analyses suggest that some small regions such as sgACC and nucleus accumbens require less control energy, and that participants with remitted depression appear easier to push into sad mood and harder to return fully to a neutral-like state, despite similar nominal target attainment. The paper’s main contribution is a control-theoretic lens on psychiatric state dynamics, not a validated intervention recipe.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it offers a decent computational language for talking about neural state transitions, control energy, and target ranking without collapsing into “connectivity changed, therefore mechanism.” It is more useful as a design scaffold than as evidence.
notes.finalDecision: Preserve as adjacent computational inspiration. Good for theory and target-ranking ideas; not yet strong translational evidence.

related.title: Closed-loop and personalized targeting
related.overview: The good neuromodulation papers are converging on a stricter standard than the field used to tolerate.

# 2026-04-28

## Theme

Today is a **state-aware targeting and control-geometry** day. The most relevant paper is **Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus**, because it actually uses a patient-specific whole-brain model to ask which targets move which abnormal state instead of treating target choice as sloganized location picking. The strongest network-control paper is **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**, because it makes stimulation geometry more realistic and shows that diffuse control can reduce transition energy dramatically. The clearest clinical adaptive paper is **Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome**, which is still only a case study but at least ties adaptation to a real biomarker and a real operational use case. The best methods paper is **Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study**, because it makes the usual personalization problem painfully concrete across nearly six hundred aging-brain anatomies.

## Short overview

The most relevant paper today is **Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus**. The authors built a tinnitus-specific digital twin brain from multimodal imaging and used more than 1.64 million virtual stimulations to map how different targets shift two abnormal whole-brain states, one more sensory-weighted and one more cognitive-default-mode weighted. The useful claim is not that tinnitus targeting is solved. The useful claim is that state-specific target choice may be the right abstraction, and the authors do at least validate their response maps against an independent repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation dataset.

The second paper is **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**. This is not a clinical trial. It is a network-control paper arguing that the usual node-by-node control assumption is physically silly for cortex and for real stimulation devices. When the authors allow inputs to spread spatially with exponential decay, state transitions require much less energy and can often be approximated with far fewer input sites. That matters because intervention logic should respect the fact that stimulation is not a perfectly local delta function.

The third paper is **Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome**. In one patient with refractory Tourette syndrome and obsessive-compulsive disorder, chronic sensing from ventral capsule or ventral striatum and centromedian-parafascicular thalamus showed circadian beta rhythms that were then used to reduce stimulation automatically during sleep. The result is still fragile single-patient evidence, but it is a respectable proof of concept for slow adaptive control driven by a clinically usable day-night signal rather than by fragile moment-to-moment detection.

The fourth paper is **Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study**. Using finite-element simulations in 590 Human Connectome Project-Aging participants, the authors show that montage, skull thickness, cerebrospinal-fluid thickness, cortical thickness, local gyrification, and sulcal depth all materially shift where current actually goes. The important read is not that one montage wins universally. It is that standardized dosing still produces highly nonstandardized electric fields.

## Ranked list

1. **Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus**  
   Directly relevant translational modeling paper. Most relevant paper today.  
   Why it matters: It treats target selection as a state-specific causal-response problem inside a subject-informed whole-brain model, then checks whether those maps predict real rTMS effects.

2. **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**  
   Adjacent but highly valuable network-control paper.  
   Why it matters: It replaces unrealistic point-input control with spatially diffuse control and shows that the geometry change itself alters what looks energetically and biologically plausible.

3. **Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome**  
   Directly relevant adaptive neuromodulation paper.  
   Why it matters: It ties adaptive DBS to a practical biomarker and to sleep-versus-wake stimulation management instead of performing adaptive theater for its own sake.

4. **Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study**  
   Directly relevant methods and targeting paper.  
   Why it matters: It gives a large-sample reminder that tDCS personalization is constrained by anatomy before it is saved by software rhetoric.

## Most relevant paper

**Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus**

This gets top rank because it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to turn target selection into an explicit dynamical-response question rather than a static lesion-or-connectivity slogan. The useful move is that it separates sensory and cognitive abnormal states, derives different causal response maps for each, and then validates those maps against real rTMS outcome variation. It is still a disease-specific paper and still model-dependent, but the framing transfers well to psychiatric and neuromodulation work more broadly.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For digital-twin targeting:** the tinnitus paper is a real framing upgrade because it asks which target perturbs which pathological state, not just which site correlates with symptoms.
- **For network control logic:** the diffuse-input paper weakens the default habit of treating brain control as independent node poking and gives a better physical prior for stimulation design.
- **For adaptive DBS:** the Tourette case is small, but it is a sensible reminder that slow circadian adaptation may be easier to deploy robustly than hyper-reactive closed-loop fantasies.
- **For tDCS targeting:** the anatomy-informed montage paper is mostly a methods result, but it should make anyone suspicious of one-size-fits-all dosing claims.
- **For repo framing:** today’s set is balanced the right way, with one translational digital-twin paper, one control-theory paper, one adaptive clinical proof of concept, and one large-sample anatomy and targeting methods paper.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The useful pattern today is that neuromodulation gets better when papers stop pretending stimulation is either perfectly local or perfectly generic. The tinnitus digital-twin study asks which target changes which abnormal state. The diffuse-input control paper shows that realistic spatial spread changes the control problem itself. The Tourette adaptive DBS case uses a slow, interpretable biomarker tied to actual sleep-wake needs instead of chasing flashy millisecond adaptivity. And the tDCS montage paper reminds us that anatomy still decides a lot of what the protocol really is. Taken together, this is a good day for state-aware and geometry-aware intervention logic.

## Category calls

### Directly relevant

- [Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus](https://cabbageland.github.io/cabbageclaw-neuro-daily-web/paper_notes/digital_twin_tinnitus_state_targets)
- [Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome](https://cabbageland.github.io/cabbageclaw-neuro-daily-web/paper_notes/circadian_adbs_tourette)
- [Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study](https://cabbageland.github.io/cabbageclaw-neuro-daily-web/paper_notes/anatomy_informed_tdcs_montage)

### Adjacent computational and network-control framing

- [Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals](https://cabbageland.github.io/cabbageclaw-neuro-daily-web/paper_notes/spatially_diffuse_connectome_control_2026)

## Inspection notes / uncertainty

- Brave Search was attempted first as required, but the Brave Search API is not configured in this environment. Discovery therefore fell back to direct Europe PMC and PubMed abstract scouting.
- **Digital twin brain reveals state-specific stimulation targets for abnormal brain dynamics in tinnitus** was inspected through the PubMed abstract and metadata. Confidence is good on the multimodal digital-twin framing, the two-state decomposition, the virtual-stimulation scale, and the existence of independent rTMS validation. Confidence is limited on the exact model-fitting details, the robustness of the gene-expression integration, and whether prediction quality would hold across other disease cohorts.
- **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals** was inspected through the PubMed abstract and metadata. Confidence is good on the core modeling move and the broad result that diffuse inputs lower required control energy. Confidence is limited on how sensitive the results are to the assumed decay kernel and to the linear control framework itself.
- **Circadian limbic and thalamic beta oscillations drive slow-adapting dual-threshold adaptive deep brain stimulation in Tourette syndrome** was inspected through the PubMed abstract and metadata. Confidence is good on the case-study design, the sleep-related adaptation logic, and the cross-target tethering setup. Confidence is low on generalizability because this is one patient with an accidental sixteen-night off-period rather than a planned controlled trial.
- **Anatomy-informed recommendations for electrode montage and shape in electrical stimulation methods: a tDCS case study** was inspected through the PubMed abstract and metadata. Confidence is good on cohort size, simulation workflow, and the main anatomical drivers of field variability. Confidence is limited on how directly these network-level electric-field differences translate to clinical or behavioral outcomes.
markdown.daily_papers/2026-03-26.md:
# 2026-03-26

## Theme

The useful neuromodulation papers today are less about raw efficacy and more about **whether the intervention logic is legible**. The strongest work either (a) ties outcome prediction to an actually recorded circuit signal, (b) makes targeting variability explicit instead of pretending scalp heuristics are precise, or (c) shows a manipulable mechanism at the cell/circuit level. The weaker work still likes grand network stories assembled from normative connectomes and retrospective aggregation.

## Short overview

Today’s strongest hit is the BNST-NAc DBS depression paper because it combines a randomized clinical design with perioperative physiology, longitudinal tracking, and a biomarker story that is at least specific enough to attack. The precision TMS modeling paper is useful because it exposes how sloppy standard dlPFC targeting still is and gives a practical individual-network targeting workflow, though it remains a targeting/modeling paper rather than an outcome trial. The tFUS rat paper is adjacent rather than translational, but it is one of the cleaner recent mechanism papers because it links parameter regime to bidirectional circuit effects and identifies a specific cell-type contribution. A depression “common therapeutic network” paper is worth noting mainly as framing/citation material; it is ambitious and interesting, but much of the causal language outruns what secondary network mapping can really support.

## Ranked list

1. **Prefrontal-bed nucleus of the stria terminalis physiological and neuropsychological biomarkers predict therapeutic outcomes in depression**  
   Directly relevant. Most relevant paper today.  
   Why it matters: It pairs psychiatric DBS with actual intracranial signal features, identifies a predictive state/readout, and links that readout to symptom and quality-of-life outcomes over months.

2. **Precision Network Modeling of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Across Individuals Suggests Therapeutic Targets and Potential for Improvement**  
   Directly relevant.  
   Why it matters: It makes a practical point the field often evades — common scalp or sgACC-anticorrelation targets do not map cleanly onto the same functional networks across people, so “personalized TMS” needs better targeting logic than slogans.

3. **Cell-Type-Specific Bidirectional Modulation of the Cortico-Thalamo-Cortical Sensory Pathway by Transcranial Focused Ultrasound (tFUS)**  
   Adjacent inspiration.  
   Why it matters: It gives parameter-dependent excitatory vs inhibitory effects with identified neuronal contributors, which is far more useful than generic ultrasound modulation claims.

4. **Distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common brain network**  
   Mostly citation material.  
   Why it matters: Potentially useful for framing cross-modality convergence, but much of the evidence is indirect network inference rather than direct intervention-level mechanism.

## Most relevant paper

**Prefrontal-bed nucleus of the stria terminalis physiological and neuropsychological biomarkers predict therapeutic outcomes in depression**

It earns the top slot because it does more than report another psychiatric DBS response rate. The paper records perioperative BNST-local physiology and frontal-BNST coupling, uses those features to predict longer-horizon outcomes, tracks the same theta biomarker longitudinally during the blinded crossover period, and ties the physiology to affective bias/anxiety measures and tractography. It is still a small refractory-depression trial, so nobody should confuse this with settled biomarker validation, but it is much closer to a testable circuit-therapeutics workflow than most depression DBS papers.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For psychiatric DBS framing:** outcome prediction tied to an implanted signal is more persuasive than anatomy-only target rhetoric. If a paper claims personalization, it should ideally specify both tract geometry and a physiological state variable.
- **For TMS targeting baselines:** scalp landmarks and even simple sgACC-anticorrelation targeting look increasingly under-specified once you inspect which higher-order network is actually being hit in an individual.
- **For ultrasound papers:** mechanistic animal work that shows directionality and cell-type mediation is still more believable than tiny human open-label efficacy stories.
- **For depression network claims:** cross-treatment “common network” stories are interesting, but they can slip from convergence analysis into causal overreach unless supported by direct perturbation/readout evidence.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The real pattern today is that the better papers are forcing neuromodulation to become more explicit about control variables. The BNST-DBS study says: here is the signal, here is how it predicts outcome, here is how it moves with stimulation. The TMS modeling paper says: here is why your supposed target is not reliably the same target across people. The tFUS paper says: here are the parameter regimes and neuronal populations behind opposite effects. That is the right direction. By contrast, the common-network depression paper is interesting synthesis but still too inferential to carry much mechanistic weight on its own.

## Category calls

### Directly relevant

- [Prefrontal-bed nucleus of the stria terminalis physiological and neuropsychological biomarkers predict therapeutic outcomes in depression](../paper_notes/bnst_nac_dbs_depression_biomarkers.md)
- [Precision Network Modeling of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Across Individuals Suggests Therapeutic Targets and Potential for Improvement](../paper_notes/precision_network_modeling_tms.md)

### Adjacent inspiration

- [Cell-Type-Specific Bidirectional Modulation of the Cortico-Thalamo-Cortical Sensory Pathway by Transcranial Focused Ultrasound (tFUS)](../paper_notes/tfus_bidirectional_corticothalamic_modulation.md)

### Mostly citation material

- **Distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common brain network** — useful for framing cross-modality convergence in depression, but heavily dependent on normative-connectome mapping and retrospective aggregation rather than direct target-engagement evidence.

## Inspection notes / uncertainty

- BNST-DBS note based on PubMed/PMC accessible text and figures; strongest evidence in this batch, but still a small refractory-depression cohort.
- Precision TMS note based mainly on abstract/figure text from PubMed/PMC-accessible article text; enough to preserve the targeting logic, not enough to overclaim on downstream clinical performance.
- tFUS note based on bioRxiv abstract only; preserved because the mechanism claim is clean and recent, but confidence should be treated as provisional until fuller inspection.
- Common-network depression paper was inspected through PubMed/PMC-accessible text; conceptually useful, but I did not promote it to a full note because the causal interpretation is looser than the title suggests.

# 2026-05-05

## Theme

Today is a **state-aware stimulation logic, patient-specific network heterogeneity, and post-pulse network reconfiguration** day. The most relevant paper is **Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity**, because it makes a strong mechanistic point that stimulation effects depend not just on local phase but on the transient whole-network state the pulse lands in. The strongest translational-control paper is **Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation**, because it upgrades adaptive DBS from threshold folklore toward explicit state estimation while staying real-time feasible. The strongest personalized-modeling paper is **Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration**, because it treats VNS response heterogeneity as a model-identification problem rather than a vague clinical trait. The adjacent network-methods paper is **Intrinsic brain network dynamics modulated by neural stimulation to cerebellum**, which is useful mostly as a reminder that stimulation can alter modular flexibility and integration structure without yielding a single tidy network prototype.

## Short overview

The most relevant paper today is **Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity**. Using connectome-based whole-brain modeling, the authors ask how the impact of a single pulse depends on both local oscillatory phase and the current large-scale functional-connectivity configuration. The useful claim is not just that stimulation is state dependent, which is already familiar. The stronger claim is that network-aware state descriptors can improve prediction of stimulation effects by up to about forty percent and that pulses can trigger whole-brain state switching. That is exactly the kind of paper that sharpens intervention logic rather than merely decorating it.

The second paper is **Bayesian time-history modeling enhances Parkinsonian motor state classification for adaptive deep brain stimulation**. In chronic at-home recordings from three Parkinson's disease patients with sensing-enabled DBS systems, the authors compare instantaneous discriminant classifiers against hidden-Markov time-history models for classifying motor state from cortical entrained gamma and subthalamic beta biomarkers. The main result is modest but real: adding time history improves hyperkinetic-state detection and smooths predictions without sacrificing real-time feasibility. The limitation is obvious, namely the tiny sample, but the control framing is still better than most adaptive-DBS decoding papers.

The third paper is **Personalized Virtual Brain Simulations and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcomes in Pediatric Epilepsy: A Multicenter Study From the CONNECTiVOS Collaboration**. Using preimplant diffusion and functional MRI from thirty-eight children with drug-resistant epilepsy, the authors fit subject-specific reduced Wong-Wang whole-brain models and compare responders with nonresponders after VNS. Nonresponders show worse model-based predictability of functional connectivity, while responders show stronger inferred inhibitory weights in thalamic, cingulate, and frontal nodes of the vagal afferent network. This is still model-dependent association rather than proof of mechanism, but it is a serious attempt to make responder heterogeneity computationally legible.

The fourth paper is **Intrinsic brain network dynamics modulated by neural stimulation to cerebellum**. Here the authors use resting-state fMRI before and after inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to right cerebellar Crus I and analyze changes in dynamic community structure. Post stimulation, network flexibility rises and the dynamic patterns remain highly individual rather than collapsing into one canonical mode. This is not a clinical paper and not a targeting recipe, but it is useful for reminding us that stimulation can change large-scale integration and segregation properties in ways that simple average-connectivity summaries may miss.

   Adjacent inspiration from network neuroscience and perturbation methods.

## Most relevant paper

**Phase-dependent stimulation response is shaped by the brain's dynamic functional connectivity**

This gets top rank because it shifts the intervention question from, "what phase was the target in," to, "what coordinated network state was the brain in when the pulse landed." That is a much better control framing. If stimulation effects depend on transient distributed connectivity and can even push the brain into another global state, then a serious closed-loop system should estimate more than a local oscillatory scalar.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For closed-loop stimulation logic:** the phase-dependent modeling paper raises the bar. Local phase alone may be too thin a state variable when distributed functional-connectivity state materially changes pulse effects.
- **For adaptive DBS:** the Bayesian motor-state paper is a useful baseline reminder that simple temporal models can add value before anyone reaches for giant black-box decoders.

# 2026-04-15

## Theme

Today is a **stop treating targeting folklore as validation** day. The strongest clinical-translational keep is **Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study**, because it is a useful corrective to the field’s habit of treating anti-subgenual targeting as if it were already settled truth. The strongest methods paper is **Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI**, because it tries to replace correlational target rhetoric with empirically evoked circuit maps. The strongest computational-network paper is **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**, which matters because most control models still pretend stimulation acts on isolated nodes even though real stimulation spreads in space.

## Short overview

The most relevant paper today is **Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study**. This is a prospective multisite observational test of one of the most repeated ideas in depression TMS: that left-DLPFC sites with stronger negative functional connectivity to subgenual cingulate should produce better antidepressant outcomes. Sixty-six patients with major depressive disorder received three to eight weeks of routine clinical left-DLPFC rTMS, with actual stimulation sites recorded by MRI neuronavigation. The cleanest result is negative. Normative subgenual-connectivity of the delivered site did **not** predict symptom improvement on its own, and most explained variance came instead from baseline anxiety and psychiatric comorbidity. That does not mean network targeting is useless. It does mean the simple anti-subgenual heuristic looks too thin for real-world heterogeneous clinics.

The second paper is **Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI**. Over more than eighty participants, the authors used personalized cortical targets intended to engage either subgenual anterior cingulate cortex or basolateral amygdala, then measured TMS-evoked BOLD responses while controlling for motion, pain, and somatosensory confounds. The useful result is not that they discovered a magic psychiatric target. It is that image-guided TMS can produce reproducible distributed downstream responses and that the resulting maps can serve as a more causal complement to resting-connectivity target stories.

The third paper is **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**. This is not a stimulation trial, but it is exactly the kind of network-control paper that improves intervention logic. The authors modify optimal-control models so inputs spread spatially with exponential distance decay instead of acting only on single nodes. Under that more realistic assumption, state transitions often require much less energy and many fewer effective input signals, and the derived input-density maps align with independent functional, metabolic, genetic, and neurochemical annotations. The paper matters because real brain stimulation is spatially blurry, and control theory that ignores that blur may be optimizing the wrong object.

A fourth paper stayed below note threshold but remains useful citation material: **Clinical utility and prospective of TMS-EEG: Updated review from an international expert group**. It is broad and competent, but it is still a review rather than a preserve-worthy mechanistic advance.

## Ranked list

1. **Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study**  
   Directly relevant. Most relevant paper today.  
   Why it matters: It pressures a widely repeated precision-TMS heuristic with a more heterogeneous real-world sample and gets a largely negative answer.

2. **Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI**  
   Directly relevant.  
   Why it matters: It generates empirically evoked downstream circuit maps instead of relying only on resting-connectivity inference.

3. **Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals**  
   Directly relevant.  
   Why it matters: It makes network control theory look more like actual stimulation physics by modeling spatial spread rather than perfectly local inputs.

4. **Clinical utility and prospective of TMS-EEG: Updated review from an international expert group**  
   Mostly citation material.  
   Why it matters: It is a reasonable field-status review, but not the kind of paper that changes intervention logic by itself.

## Most relevant paper

**Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study**

This is the top paper because negative translational results are unusually valuable when they hit a dominant targeting story. The field has spent years acting as if anti-subgenual connectivity was already an operationally robust rule for depression TMS. This study does not kill that idea, but it does show that once you leave cleaner single-site samples and step into a more clinically messy population, normative connectivity alone explains very little. That is exactly the kind of correction worth preserving.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For depression-TMS framing:** today’s lead paper weakens the habit of talking as if anti-subgenual targeting is already a reliable standalone personalization rule in routine practice.
- **For causal-targeting logic:** the interleaved TMS/fMRI paper is useful because it offers stimulation-evoked circuit maps that can pressure-test connectivity-based target claims.
- **For network-control modeling:** the spatially diffuse control paper matters because single-node input assumptions are often a bad proxy for how real stimulation spreads through cortex and white matter.
- **For future baselines:** papers that claim precision targeting should probably be compared against heterogeneous clinical covariates and not just against prettier connectivity maps.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish overconfident targeting narratives. The depression-TMS cohort study says a famous normative-connectivity heuristic is much less robust in real clinics than people often imply. The interleaved TMS/fMRI paper says if you want to talk about circuits, you should measure stimulation-evoked circuit consequences rather than stopping at resting correlations. And the spatially diffuse control paper says control theory should stop pretending that stimulation enters the brain as perfectly local node-wise impulses. Overall lesson: better intervention logic will require more causal measurement, more realistic control assumptions, and more respect for clinical heterogeneity.

# 2026-04-05

## Theme

Today is a **personalization claims under stress** day. The strongest paper is the Brain study **Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study**, because it uses multi-year implanted recordings to ask a question the field keeps dodging: can we see response trajectories early enough to guide therapy rather than waiting passively for slow clinical drift. The most translationally provocative paper is the Research Square preprint **Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy**, which is ambitious and clinically attractive but currently too abstract-level and too preprint-dependent to trust without caution. The most interesting computational paper is the arXiv preprint **Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model**, which is strong on scale and framing but still lives in the danger zone where personalized virtual brains can become high-gloss response prediction theater.

## Short overview

The most relevant paper today is **Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study**. The valuable part is not that it found yet another biomarker. The valuable part is that it used four years of longitudinal anterior thalamic recordings from twenty-two patients to examine whether response to anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation leaves a durable physiological trace rather than only a delayed clinical one. According to the abstract, responders progressively shift toward higher-frequency anterior thalamic activity and away from lower-frequency activity, and simple high-to-low spectral ratios can discriminate eventual clinical outcome early. That does not prove a ready-made adaptive controller, but it is the right level of question: can the implant tell you whether therapy is converging or stalling before you waste months.

The second keep-worthy paper is **Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy**. This is exactly the sort of paper that needs both attention and skepticism. The appealing claim is clear: a deep-learning framework integrates thirty-three EEG features in forty-five pediatric patients to derive a personalized pre-ictal threshold, then uses that threshold to trigger transcranial temporal interference stimulation in thirteen patients and six macaques. The paper says the personalized interventions suppressed seizure onset. If that holds up, it is a serious advance in proactive seizure control. But almost everything important is still unresolved from accessible text alone: exact detector calibration, false-alarm burden, stimulation geometry, comparison against simpler baselines, and what "suppressed" means operationally.

The third preserve-worthy paper is **Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model**. This is a big claim paper, but it is not obviously empty. The authors pretrain a generative virtual-brain model on a large resting-state fMRI collection, then finetune on Parkinson cohorts receiving temporal interference or deep brain stimulation and use counterfactual healthy-versus-pathological state estimates to predict treatment response. The headline metrics are strong, including external and prospective validation in small additional cohorts. The reason to keep it is not that virtual-brain foundation models are automatically trustworthy. The reason is that it reframes outcome prediction around patient-specific state transition modeling rather than only static biomarkers. Still, this could collapse into sophisticated overfitting if the individualized generative machinery is less identifiable than the paper suggests.

A fourth paper that stayed in scope but below the preserve threshold is **Phase estimation with autoregressive padding, or PEAP: addressing inaccuracies and biases in EEG analysis**. It may end up mattering more than some flashier intervention studies because real-time phase-targeted stimulation is only as good as the phase estimator. The paper reports that common methods are systematically biased and that PEAP improves accuracy while reducing edge artifacts. That is useful and probably real. I kept it just below the note threshold today because the immediate translational consequence is methodological hygiene rather than a direct intervention result.

## Ranked list

1. **Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study**  
   Directly relevant. Most relevant paper today.  
   Why it matters: It asks whether long-horizon implanted thalamic signals can forecast and track deep brain stimulation response early enough to support biomarker-guided optimization rather than blind waiting.

2. **Pre-ictal signature-guided individualized closed-loop tTIS suppresses seizures onset in pediatric epilepsy**  
   Directly relevant.  
   Why it matters: It pushes noninvasive seizure control toward pre-emptive, patient-specific triggering instead of generic reactive stimulation, but the current evidence is still too preprint-fragile to accept at face value.

3. **Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model**  
   Adjacent but preserve-worthy.  
   Why it matters: It offers a mechanistic-looking response-prediction frame based on individualized state modeling rather than a flat classifier, which is exactly the kind of promise that deserves close scrutiny.

4. **Phase estimation with autoregressive padding (PEAP): addressing inaccuracies and biases in EEG analysis**  
   Adjacent inspiration.  
   Why it matters: If phase-targeted EEG-TMS or oscillation-locked stimulation pipelines are biased at the segment edge, then some apparent precision-neuromodulation results may be partly analysis artifact.

## Most relevant paper

**Intracranial biomarkers for anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation in epilepsy: a long-term observational study**

This is the top paper because it is trying to solve a real translational bottleneck instead of inventing another decorative biomarker. Anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation for drug-refractory epilepsy often works slowly and unevenly, which leaves clinicians with weak feedback while programming therapy. The paper analyzes longitudinal implanted recordings across four years and reports that responders show progressive increases in beta-one and gamma power with decreases in delta and theta power, while high-to-low spectral ratios such as beta-one over theta help discriminate eventual outcomes early. That is still observational and biomarker logic can go fake fast, but the study at least connects physiology to the practical question of whether therapy is converging.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For epilepsy DBS:** the Brain paper suggests that long-term anterior thalamic spectral trajectories may be a more actionable response marker than raw seizure counts alone, which could affect how adaptive or biomarker-guided programming is framed.
- **For noninvasive seizure control:** the tTIS preprint is interesting because it moves from generic closed-loop rhetoric toward explicitly personalized pre-ictal triggering, but it now needs brutal baseline comparison and false-positive accounting.
- **For computational neuromodulation:** the virtual-brain Parkinson paper raises the bar for response-prediction claims by coupling prediction to counterfactual state modeling rather than plain classification, but it also raises the identifiability and leakage stakes.
- **For methods skepticism:** the PEAP paper is a reminder that some precision-timing claims may be only as valid as the phase-estimation pipeline underneath them.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s pattern is that personalization only matters if the control logic survives contact with time, noise, and heterogeneity. The best paper is the anterior thalamic DBS study because it deals with slow therapeutic drift and asks whether implanted physiology can reveal response trajectories early. The pediatric tTIS paper is ambitious and worth preserving precisely because it could be important, but right now it reads like a high-upside claim in need of a much harsher methods audit. The virtual-brain Parkinson paper is the right kind of computational ambition — state modeling instead of decorative prediction — but it is still at serious risk of becoming elegant overfitting if the model’s mechanistic interpretation outruns its evidence.

# 2026-03-28

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is that **good neuromodulation papers are getting more explicit about circuit response and less convincing when they overpromise personalization**. The best paper is a serious individual-level DBS neuroimaging study that actually tries to map what stimulation is doing over time and across frequencies. The most useful clinical paper is a negative rTMS trial in chronic pain showing that a plausible connectivity-based targeting idea did *not* beat standard M1 targeting. The most interesting hardware preprint is a deep-stimulation relay concept that is clever but still very early.

## Short overview

The most worth-preserving paper today is **Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans** because it goes after a question the field keeps hand-waving around: what circuits does DBS modulate in actual individuals, under different frequencies, over time? **Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided randomized trial** is valuable precisely because it is a negative result: global connectivity-guided targeting did not improve outcomes, which is useful pressure against decorative “personalization” rhetoric. **A minimally invasive floating-wire interface for transcranial deep brain stimulation** is adjacent inspiration rather than near-term translational evidence; the idea is technically interesting, but the current evidence is simulations, benchtop validation, and rodent motor-threshold work.

## Ranked list

1. **Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans**  
   Directly relevant. Most relevant paper today.  
   Why it matters: It combines unusually deep longitudinal fMRI phenotyping with actual DBS parameter variation in individual Parkinson patients, which is much closer to usable circuit mapping than the usual group-average story about “DBS normalizes networks.”

2. **Personalizing neuromodulation for chronic pain: A connectivity-guided randomized trial**  
   Directly relevant.  
   Why it matters: A useful null. Connectivity-based target allocation using the authors’ global EEG-connectivity metric did not beat standard M1 stimulation, which is exactly the kind of result the field needs if it wants biomarker claims to mean anything.

3. **A minimally invasive floating-wire interface for transcranial deep brain stimulation**  
   Adjacent inspiration.  
   Why it matters: The relay-wire idea is clever because it tries to steal some of DBS’s focality without fully implanting a pulse-generator-plus-lead system, but the evidence is still preclinical and safety/long-term stability remain wide open.

4. **Network-targeted TMS modulates task-related striatal activity during motor skill learning**  
   Sounds relevant but weak.  
   Why it matters: It shows some task-evoked striatal modulation after DLPFC cTBS, but no clear behavioral gain and a fairly conventional coordinate-based targeting setup, so the translational leap would be premature.

## Most relevant paper

**Circuit response to neuromodulation characterized with simultaneous deep brain stimulation and precision neuroimaging in humans**

This gets the top slot because it does real mechanistic work rather than packaging. The authors use a 3-T MRI-compatible STN-DBS system, scan 14 Parkinson patients longitudinally for a year, and collect enough imaging in each person to estimate individual functional networks and stimulation responses under OFF, high-frequency, low-frequency, and variable-frequency conditions. The useful part is not just that DBS helps symptoms — we already know that — but that they identify separable pallidal and motor-cortical circuit responses with distinct time and frequency dependence, and they argue that individualized target-cortical connectivity can predict and track motor outcomes. It is still Parkinson’s disease rather than psychiatry, and the sample is not huge, but it is a serious template for how circuit-level neuromodulation mapping should be done.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

- **For invasive neuromodulation:** this raises the bar from “DBS changes connectivity somehow” to repeated individual-level circuit mapping under multiple stimulation regimes.
- **For personalization claims:** the chronic-pain rTMS trial is a healthy corrective. A personalization story based on a plausible biomarker is still not good enough if the chosen metric does not improve outcomes.
- **For closed-loop / adaptive logic:** the DBS paper supports the idea that stimulation effects are frequency- and timescale-specific across distinct circuits, which is the kind of structure adaptive controllers should exploit rather than collapsing everything into a single scalar biomarker.
- **For device/platform thinking:** FLOATES is interesting as an intervention concept, but right now it is more a provocative engineering direction than a treatment paper.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The honest read today is that neuromodulation gets more interesting when papers expose circuit structure and less interesting when they sell targeting heuristics as personalization. The DBS precision-neuroimaging study is worth keeping because it combines deep longitudinal measurement with parameter variation and individual network estimation. The chronic-pain trial is worth keeping because it shows a reasonable connectivity-guided targeting idea can still fail clinically. FLOATES is worth remembering as a clever minimally invasive concept, but not yet as evidence that deep noninvasive-ish stimulation has solved its core translational problems.
